title: No, you didn’t miss jury duty!
summary: The phone rings and the caller identifies himself as a Deputy U.S. Marshal. He states that you missed jury duty, a judge has issued a ...
body_text: No, you didn’t miss jury duty! Posted on Jul 23rd, 2026 The phone rings and the caller identifies himself as a Deputy U.S. Marshal. He states that you missed jury duty, a judge has issued a warrant for your arrest, and that the only way to avoid being taken into custody is to resolve the matter immediately. Within seconds, a text message arrives with an image of what looks like an official federal warrant. This is not a hypothetical. It is a real scam, and it is spreading quickly across the country. The following account is based on an actual incident involving a family member of one of our cybersecurity team members, recounted here to illustrate exactly how the scam unfolds and why it works. How the Scam Played Out The target received a call from a local area code. The caller claimed to be a Deputy U.S. Marshal and said that a warrant had been issued for missing jury duty. Almost simultaneously, a text arrived containing an image of a fraudulent arrest warrant. The caller already knew the target’s name and phone number, and cited an address where the target had lived years earlier. When the target pointed out that the address was outdated, the caller didn’t miss a beat; he simply replied that this must be where the paperwork had gone wrong. It was a small, confident correction, and it was enough to keep the story believable. The caller then explained that the “fine” was $18,000, but that the judge was willing to be flexible. He asked the target to check their bank balance to see how much could be sent right away. Payment, he said, could be made through Cash App or Zelle. When the target, who was near a police station at the time, offered to simply walk in and sort the matter out in person, the caller’s tone changed. He became insistent, warned that local police could not be trusted, and pressed harder for immediate payment. That shift was the clearest signal that something was wrong. The target ended the call and contacted a family member with a law enforcement background instead of complying. Why This Scam Is Effective What makes this scam dangerous isn’t the fake document. It’s the person on the other end of the line. These are not the poorly worded, easily dismissed scam attempts of years past. The callers are composed, articulate, and unhurried. They have enough personal information about the target to make the story plausible, and the warrant images they send are convincingly designed to resemble authentic court documents. The entire interaction is engineered to produce one outcome: panic. Fear short-circuits careful thinking. It replaces “let me verify this” with “how do I make this go away right now?” and that reaction is precisely what the scammer is counting on. What to Know Courts do not call demanding immediate payment to avoid arrest. Legitimate legal processes do not work this way. No law enforcement agency accepts fines or bail through Cash App, Zelle, Venmo, gift cards, or cryptocurrency. Any request for payment through these channels is a red flag on its own. No legitimate official will ask you to keep the matter secret or avoid contacting local police. Secrecy is a control tactic, not a legal requirement. A real warrant is never resolved by sending money through a mobile payment app. Caller ID cannot be trusted. Scammers routinely spoof local numbers, including ones that appear to belong to government offices or courthouses. What to Do If You Receive One of These Calls Do not provide personal information. Do not send money, in any form. Do not click links or open attachments sent to you as “proof.” Hang up immediately. Verify independently. Contact your local police department, your county clerk of courts, or the court directly, using a phone number you look up yourself rather than one provided by the caller. If you or someone you know receives a call like this, the safest response is the simplest one: stop, disengage, and verify through channels you control. title: Finward Bancorp Acquisition
summary: First Financial Bancorp. (“First Financial”) has agreed to acquire Finward Bancorp (“Finward”), the holding company for Peoples…...
body_text: Finward Bancorp Acquisition July 21, 2026 4:30pm EDT Download as PDF First Financial Bancorp. (“First Financial”) has agreed to acquire Finward Bancorp (“Finward”), the holding company for Peoples Bank, headquartered in Munster, Indiana Strategically expands First Financial's presence in northwest Indiana and Chicago, with the addition of a low cost core deposit franchise and 24 locations Finward has approximately $2.0 billion in assets, $1.7 billion in deposits, $1.5 billion in loans and $412 million in assets under management Transaction is expected to be approximately 5% accretive to First Financial’s earnings per share MUNSTER, Ind.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- First Financial Bancorp. (Nasdaq: FFBC) and Finward Bancorp (Nasdaq: FNWD) jointly announced today that they have entered into an agreement by which First Financial will acquire Munster-based Finward in an all-stock transaction, further expanding First Financial’s presence in the economically robust Chicagoland market with a strong core deposit franchise including 24 financial centers and a 116 year presence in the Northwest Indiana and Chicago markets. Combined with the 15 retail locations from First Financial’s recent acquisition in the Chicagoland market, the Finward acquisition enhances First Financial’s market presence and increases its pro forma deposits in the Chicago metropolitan statistical area by 75% to over $4 billion. "The addition of Finward Bancorp and Peoples Bank is expected to strategically expand First Financial’s ability to serve the consumers and businesses of the Chicagoland and Northwest Indiana markets. We are excited to partner with a bank with a similar operating philosophy and strong credit culture,” said Archie Brown, President and Chief Executive Officer of First Financial Bank. “We have built an impressive combination of retail and commercial banking services, wealth management services, and specialty banking solutions, complemented by our client-centered, community-focused business model, that offers an alternative to larger banks. To demonstrate our further commitment to Chicago and Northwest Indiana, First Financial has committed to donate $500,000 to its Foundation for the benefit of local organizations in the communities served by Finward, in addition to the $1 million we donated to the Foundation when we entered the Chicago market with the completed acquisition of BankFinancial Corporation in January 2026.” Upon completion of the transaction, Finward’s consumer, trust/wealth management and commercial credit lines of business will be incorporated into First Financial’s respective business lines, and Peoples Bank employees will become First Financial associates. “This partnership represents an exciting next chapter for our organization and the communities we serve,” said Benjamin Bochnowski, Chief Executive Officer of Peoples Bank. “First Financial shares our deep commitment to customers, employees, shareholders, and the communities that have placed their trust in us for more than 100 years. Together, we are accelerating our common strategy to better serve the Chicagoland and Northwest Indiana markets. We are creating a stronger regional banking franchise with expanded capabilities, greater resources, and a sharper focus on delivering exceptional service. We are confident this partnership will create meaningful opportunities for our customers and employees, while preserving the community-centered values that have defined our organization for generations.” Through this addition, First Financial continues its recent period of growth, including the recent acquisitions of Westfield Bancorp in Northeast Ohio and BankFinancial Corporation in Chicago, and its commercial banking expansion into Chicago, Cleveland and Grand Rapids. First Financial’s Midwestern base includes Chicago, IL; Cincinnati, Dayton, Cleveland and Columbus, OH; Indianapolis, IN; and Louisville, KY. The acquisition of Finward enhances First Financial’s existing Chicagoland footprint that includes its commercial loan production office in Fulton Market; the Agile Premium Finance division in Lincolnshire, IL; and Bannockburn Capital Markets in downtown Chicago. Additionally in the area, First Financial offers retail and business banking solutions in Northwest Indiana and Northeast Illinois. Transaction Terms Under the terms of the agreement, each outstanding share of Finward common stock will be converted into the right to receive 1.35 shares of First Financial common stock, valuing the transaction at approximately $208 million, based on First Financial’s closing stock price on July 20, 2026. The transaction is expected to be approximately 5% accretive to First Financial’s earnings per share, and First Financial’s tangible book value per share (“TBV”) at closing is estimated to be only slightly diluted (0.4% dilution) with an anticipated TBV earnback of 0.6 years. The merger agreement has been unanimously approved by the Boards of Directors of First Financial and Finward. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to satisfaction of customary closing conditions, regulatory approvals and approval of Finward’s shareholders. Transaction Advisors Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC is serving as financial advisor to First Financial. Stephens Inc. is serving as financial advisor to Finward and rendered a fairness opinion to Finward’s Board of Directors. Squire Patton Boggs, (US) LLP is serving as legal counsel to First Financial. Barack Ferrazzano Kirschbaum & Nagelberg LLP is serving as legal counsel to Finward. Important Additional Information about the Transaction and Where to Find It In connection with the proposed transaction, First Financial intends to file with the SEC a Registration Statement on Form S-4 (the “Registration Statement”) to register the shares of First Financial common stock to be issued in connection with the proposed transaction. The Registration Statement will include a proxy statement of Finward and a prospectus of First Financial (the “Proxy Statement/Prospectus”), and First Financial and Finward may file with the SEC other relevant documents concerning the proposed transaction. BEFORE MAKING ANY VOTING OR INVESTMENT DECISION, INVESTORS AND SHAREHOLDERS ARE URGED TO READ THE REGISTRATION STATEMENT AND PROXY STATEMENT/PROSPECTUS REGARDING THE PROPOSED TRANSACTION IN THEIR ENTIRETY WHEN THEY BECOME AVAILABLE AND ANY OTHER RELEVANT DOCUMENTS FILED WITH THE SEC, AS WELL AS ANY AMENDMENTS OR SUPPLEMENTS TO THOSE DOCUMENTS, BECAUSE THEY WILL CONTAIN IMPORTANT INFORMATION ABOUT FIRST FINANCIAL, FINWARD AND THE PROPOSED TRANSACTION AND RELATED MATTERS. A copy of the Registration Statement, Proxy Statement/Prospectus, as well as other filings containing information about First Financial and Finward, may be obtained, free of charge, at the SEC’s website ( www.sec.gov ) when they are filed. Copies of documents filed with the SEC by First Financial will be made available free of charge in the "Investor Relations" section of First Financial's website, https://www.bankatfirst.com/about/investor-relations.html . Copies of documents filed with the SEC by Finward will be made available free of charge in the "Investor Relations" section of Finward's website, https://www.investorrelations.ibankpeoples.com . The information on First Financial’s and Finward’s websites is not, and shall not be deemed to be, a part of this communication or incorporated into other filings either company makes with the SEC. Participants in Solicitation Finward and its directors, executive officers, management and employees may be deemed to be participants in the solicitation of proxies in respect of the Merger. Information concerning Finward’s participants is set forth in the Proxy Statement, dated April 3, 2026, for Finward’s 2026 annual meeting of shareholders as filed with the SEC on Schedule 14A. Additional information regarding the participants in the solicitation of proxies in respect of the proposed transaction and interests of participants of Finward in the solicitation of proxies in respect of the Merger will be included in the Registration Statement and Proxy Statement/Prospectus to be filed with the SEC. Free copies of these documents, when available, may be obtained as described in the preceding paragraph. About First Financial Bancorp. First Financial Bancorp. is a Cincinnati, Ohio based bank holding company. As of June 30, 2026, First Financial had $22.4 billion in assets, $13.7 billion in loans, $17.6 billion in deposits and $3.0 billion in shareholders’ equity. First Financial’s subsidiary, First Financial Bank, founded in 1863, provides banking and financial services products through its six lines of business: Commercial, Retail Banking, Investment Commercial Real Estate, Mortgage Banking, Commercial Finance and Wealth Management. These business units provide traditional banking services to business and retail clients. Wealth Management provides wealth planning, portfolio management, trust and estate, brokerage and retirement plan services and had approximately $4.6 billion in assets under management as of June 30, 2026. First Financial operated 151 full service banking centers as of June 30, 2026, located in Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and Illinois, while the Commercial Finance business lends into targeted industry verticals on a nationwide basis. In 2025, First Financial Bank received its second consecutive Outstanding rating from the Federal Reserve for its performance under the Community Reinvestment Act and was recognized as a Gallup Exceptional Workplace Award winner, one of only 70 Gallup clients worldwide to receive this designation. Additional information about First Financial, including its products, services and banking locations, is available at www.bankatfirst.com . About Finward Bancorp Finward Bancorp is a locally managed and independent financial holding company headquartered in Munster, Indiana, whose activities are primarily limited to holding the stock of Peoples Bank. Peoples Bank provides a wide range of personal, business, electronic and wealth management financial services from its 24 locations in Lake and Porter Counties in Northwest Indiana and Chicagoland. Finward Bancorp’s common stock is quoted on The NASDAQ Stock Market, LLC under the symbol FNWD. The website ibankpeoples.com provides information on Peoples Bank’s products and services, and Finward Bancorp’s investor relations. body_text: View All News Chaco and Billy Strings Team Up for a Limited-Edition Collection Inspired by Music, Michigan Roots, and Life on the Road July 27, 2026 The Billy Strings x Chaco collaboration drops July 27, featuring limited-edition, Billy-designed styles and a show-only special available at just two tour stops Grand Rapids, MI, July 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Chaco , leading outdoor footwear brand, has teamed up with Grammy-winning artist Billy Strings to release a limited-edition sandal collaboration rooted in music, river culture, and nights that turn into mornings. Launching July 27 on chacos.com , the collection brings together two communities with shared roots and a deep love for the outdoors. The collection features limited-edition Z/Sandals and dog gear inspired by the iconic artwork from Billy Strings’ 2017 album Turmoil & Tinfoil. Made in Michigan, like Billy Strings himself, the collaboration celebrates a shared origin story and a connection to the places that shape both the artist and the brand. From riverbanks to late-night sets, the collection is grounded in real moments. Like bluegrass tradition, they’re made with heart and intention, built to last, and passed down with pride. “Billy has built something real with his fans, and that kind of connection mirrors what we see in our own community,” said Rose Fulbright, Chaco Marketing Director. “This partnership is about showing up for those shared experiences, whether that is at a show, on the trail, or back at the creek.” Known for high-energy performances, Billy Strings has become one of the most beloved artists in bluegrass today. His music is shaped by the people and places he grew up around, bringing an authenticity that carries through into this collaboration. The Billy Strings x Chaco collection includes two sandal styles available online, along with one special colorway that will be sold only at two shows: Bethel Woods in New York (July 31 - August 1) and Ionia, Michigan (August 28 - August 29). To celebrate the launch, the partnership will extend beyond product into live experiences on the road, with Chaco hosting activations at both shows and giving fans a chance to shop the exclusive pair in person. The Billy Strings x Chaco limited-edition collection will be available beginning July 27 at chacos.com , with the show-only style available exclusively at Bethel Woods and Ionia while supplies last. About Chaco Born on the river in 1989, Chaco, a division of Wolverine Worldwide, Inc. (NYSE: WWW), builds premium footwear for the outdoor-minded. The brand's iconic Z/sandals are repairable at ReChaco and more than 20,000 sandals a year are kept out of landfills every year. Plus, as a result of the brand's proprietary LUVSEAT™ foot bed, the American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA) has awarded the Seal of Acceptance to all Chaco footwear styles. The APMA Seal is intended to raise awareness by identifying products of exceptional quality that are manufactured with comfort, health, and safety in mind. Simply put, Chaco is fit for adventure. Please visit us at www.chacos.com , Facebook: Chaco, Instagram: ChacoFootwear, TikTok: ChacoFootwear. About Billy Strings Raised in Michigan and now based in Nashville, Billy Strings is one of music’s most compelling artists, acclaimed for his boundary-pushing musicianship and dynamic live performances. Strings’ highly anticipated forthcoming album, So Much For Goodbyes—produced with T Bone Burnett—finds him channeling a deeply personal period into his most musically mature and reflective body of work to date. The new record arrives amid a career-defining run for Strings, whom GQ hails as “the hottest roots-music phenomenon in decades,” while Pitchfork calls him a “bluegrass wunderkind.” Strings earned his third Grammy Award and second consecutive win for Best Bluegrass Album at the 68th Annual Grammy Awards with Highway Prayers, which debuted at No. 1 on Billboard’s all-genre Top Album Sales chart, becoming the first bluegrass album in 22 years to achieve the feat. In addition to his solo work, Strings has collaborated across genres with artists including Kacey Musgraves, Primus, Luke Combs, Cryptopsy, Willie Nelson and Tony Trischka, among others, and recently contributed a cover of “If You’re Gonna Be Dumb, You Gotta Be Tough” for the upcoming film Jackass: Best and Last. Since his 2017 debut, Strings has earned widespread recognition, including three Grammy Awards, two back-to-back Artist of the Year at the Americana Music Awards, four-time Entertainer of the Year at the International Bluegrass Music Awards, Best New Headliner at the 2022 Pollstar Awards and Breakthrough Artist of the Pandemic at the 2021 Pollstar Awards. Known for his electric live shows, Strings has performed countless sold-out dates worldwide and will continue to tour through this summer. title: PPL Recognized Among United Way’s Most Generous Corporate Partners
summary: In recognition of PPL Corporation’s ongoing commitment to giving back and supporting the communities it serves, United Way Worldwide has named PPL a President’s Circle member in its Leading Corporate Partner program, which recognizes the network’s most generous corporate partners. United Way of Greater Lehigh Valley, the local United Way that serves PPL’s headquarters community, […]
body_text: In recognition of PPL Corporation’s ongoing commitment to giving back and supporting the communities it serves, United Way Worldwide has named PPL a President’s Circle member in its Leading Corporate Partner program, which recognizes the network’s most generous corporate partners. United Way of Greater Lehigh Valley, the local United Way that serves PPL’s headquarters community, nominated PPL for the honor. “At the PPL Foundation, we believe strong communities are built through collaboration and shared investment,” said Lissette Santana, President of the PPL Foundation. “Our partnership with United Way helps connect our employees’ generosity with trusted local organizations that are working every day to address critical needs and improve quality of life across the regions we serve.” PPL employees and retirees, together with matching contributions from PPL’s affiliated foundations, pledged $10 million during the company’s annual employee-led charitable giving campaign in 2025. These contributions support more than 500 local nonprofit organizations in communities served by PPL’s utilities in Kentucky, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island, with local United Ways helping to ensure funds are directed to areas of greatest need. “Welcoming PPL into United Way Worldwide’s Leading Corporate Partner program is a milestone and a reflection of the extraordinary partnership we have built,” said Caitlin Wagner, Senior Director, Global Corporate Partnership and Development, United Way Worldwide. “The recognition reflects decades of collaboration, shared purpose, and meaningful investment in creating stronger, more resilient communities – both in Greater Lehigh Valley where PPL is based – and across the country.” “PPL exemplifies community leadership in every way. When our communities are in crisis or our residents need support, we know that we can count on the team at PPL. We are so grateful for their years of partnership and trust, and we will continue to create real impact in the communities we serve together,” added Marci Lesko, President and Chief Executive Officer, United Way of the Greater Lehigh Valley. PPL’s partnership with United Way is deeply rooted. Each year, more than 1,000 PPL employees also volunteer during United Way’s Day of Caring. July 23, 2026

title: Sharon AI Appoints Melissa Anastasiou as Chief Legal Officer
summary: NEW YORK, July 23rd, 2026 -- Sharon AI Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: SHAZ) and its subsidiaries (“Sharon AI” or “the Company”), a leading Australian Neocloud, today
body_text: NEW YORK, July 23rd, 2026 — Sharon AI Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: SHAZ) and its subsidiaries (“Sharon AI” or “the Company”), a leading Australian Neocloud, today announced the appointment of Melissa Anastasiou as Chief Legal Officer (CLO). This appointment further strengthens Sharon AI’s executive leadership team as it continues to scale its AI Cloud platform and sovereign AI infrastructure. Melissa brings more than two decades of experience across legal, finance and governance. Her appointment bolsters the leadership, risk oversight and enterprise readiness required to support disciplined execution of the Company’s long-term growth strategy. Melissa joins Sharon AI following more than 16 years at Spark New Zealand, where she served as Executive Group General Counsel and Commercial Director. During her tenure, she advised the Board and Executive Leadership Team on corporate governance, mergers and acquisitions, regulatory, privacy and cyber matters together with digital transformation. She also chaired Spark’s AI & Data Ethics Committee, leading the development of enterprise AI governance and responsible data frameworks. As Chief Legal Officer, Melissa will lead Sharon AI’s legal, governance and compliance functions, with a focus on regulatory discipline, responsible AI practices and risk management as the business scales. James Manning, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder of Sharon AI, said, “Melissa is an exceptional leader with deep experience supporting one of Australasia’s largest and most complex technology organisations. Her appointment reflects our commitment to building a leadership team capable of supporting customers, partners and investors as AI becomes critical national infrastructure.” “As demand for sovereign AI infrastructure continues to accelerate, organisations expect world-class governance and operational excellence. Melissa significantly strengthens our ability to meet those expectations and position Sharon AI for its next phase of growth.” Melissa Anastasiou, Chief Legal Officer at Sharon AI, said, “Artificial intelligence is transforming every industry, creating significant opportunities alongside new legal and governance requirements. My focus will be on building the legal and governance foundations that will support responsible execution and long-term growth.” The appointment is part of Sharon AI’s investment in building one of the region’s leading AI infrastructure teams. As the Company expands its AI cloud platform and sovereign AI capabilities, Sharon AI is attracting experienced executives from some of Australia and New Zealand’s most respected technology organisations, creating high-value local jobs while building deep expertise across finance, legal and AI infrastructure. This investment in local leadership and technical talent is intended to support Sharon AI’s ability to serve a sophisticated customer base across Australia and internationally, while maintaining the governance and security standards expected of critical AI infrastructure. title: A Billion-dollar Playbook
summary: Nutrien surpasses $1 billion in procurement with Indigenous partners, suppliers
body_text: Ten years ago, the need to increase Indigenous participation in the potash industry was clear. The path to get there was not. “We asked our suppliers to help find solutions,” says Josh Dodd, Nutrien’s Director of Procurement – Potash, “and they delivered in a big way.” Armed with Nutrien’s “Indigenous Content Playbook” as a guide, long-time suppliers and entrepreneurial Indigenous leaders began experimenting with different models to build business partnerships, encourage employment, and support training and mentorship programs. As a result, Saskatchewan’s potash supply chain is now more diverse, secure and sustainable. “The $1 billion milestone reflects the efforts and innovative thinking of our Indigenous partners, our suppliers and our company,” said Trevor Berg, Nutrien’s Senior Vice President, Potash Operations. “We recognized a need for change and our partners – Indigenous and non-Indigenous – worked together to reshape the potash supply chain. It’s a team approach that continues to make the potash industry in Saskatchewan stronger and global food security more achievable.” In 2020, Nutrien set a target of “25 x 25” – that by 2025, at least 25 percent of the local, relevant spend in the potash operating segment would be with Indigenous-owned suppliers, or suppliers who have at least 15 percent Indigenous employment. The company blew by that target in each of the past three years, with more than 30 percent of the relevant potash spend involving suppliers who met those criteria. In total, Nutrien awarded $1.1 billion in potash procurement spending to qualified suppliers between 2020-2024, including $567 million – more than 50 percent – to Indigenous-owned companies. The dollar figure, however, tells only part of the story. “The relationship reset is what’s really powerful,” explains Julie Ann Wriston, Nutrien’s Director of Indigenous Relations. “There has been an earnest effort by our partners and our company to step out and do something proactive that has actual impact. And that’s happening, thanks to our suppliers.” Moving Ore and Shifting Attitudes The changing dynamic has taken hold inside and outside the company. In 2017, Saskatoon Tribal Council established STC Industrial (STCI) as a means of generating own-source revenue and creating employment opportunities through economic development. “We didn’t own a hammer, or a ladder and we didn’t have a contract,” recalls Shaun Howdle, President and CEO of STCI. “It was very much a start-up entrepreneurial model. But we had relationships and subcontracting agreements to get our people employment and build technical capacity.” Initially, STCI began working on underground conveyor structures at Lanigan with the support of existing fabricators, including Keys Welding Service (Keys). Within three years, STCI gained the expertise and financial strength to purchase Keys and bring that capacity fully in house. Meeting Nutrien’s requirements for safety, reliability and competitive pricing, however, can be challenging for even large-scale, long-term suppliers. The cyclical timing of deliveries, fluctuating steel prices and a global pandemic made these challenges even greater for a relatively new entity working to train its people for the industry. Cody Kennedy, Chief Mine Engineer at Lanigan, recognized that Nutrien would need a different level of teamwork to give STCI/Keys a proper opportunity to address the needs of the site. Through discussions and the collaborative efforts of Lanigan General Manager Rob Jackson; Senior Manager, Procurement Operations Jaime Aamodt; and other key stakeholders, the site and STCI/Keys signed longer-term agreements that allow the supplier to better plan its labour and input needs. “We order miles of conveyor structure every year – thousands of tons of metal specifically designed to our application underground,” says Kennedy. “And we were looking at basically doubling those quantities over the next seven years. “To be fair to them, we needed to go beyond a spot contract. We needed to hammer out a commitment – with stipulations on quality, stipulations on schedule and estimated price – that let them optimize the way they plan to ensure Lanigan got the right product at the right time.” An initial two-year agreement signed in 2021 was renewed in 2023, with negotiations on a further extension currently underway. STCI/Keys’ performance over the past several years has enabled it to expand its operations, adding more employees and new services, including a powder-coating paint line to finish materials before they leave the manufacturing plant. “They’ve become competitive with their peers in the industry, which is a great thing,” says Kennedy. “It’s difficult to grow and mature into an organization that can supply the mining industry. You’re competing against big guys that are entrenched for decades. And they’ve been able to do that.” Howdle says the initiative from Nutrien to encourage partnerships while allowing flexibility to find workable solutions has been a key foundation for growth. “The biggest thing I give Nutrien credit for is understanding a true partnership as opposed to a supplier-buyer relationship,” says Howdle. “We’ve been very open with them – “This is what we need. This is what our structure is...” And they're able to work with us and say, “Okay, we need to hit these objectives and this is why…” That's a true partnership model.” Evolving the Playbook The experiences of the past decade informed updates to Nutrien’s Indigenous Content Playbook. The updated playbook, which is available here , reflects changes in the environment, industry and supply chain since the initial release almost a decade ago. Lee Price, Nutrien’s Manager, Indigenous Supply Chain - Potash, says the efforts of suppliers across the industry have been essential to the success of the program and into reshaping the opportunities for Indigenous people and businesses. The evolution of the STCI/Keys relationship with Nutrien is just one example of supply-chain partners working together and with Nutrien to strengthen the industry in Saskatchewan. “There was reciprocity – finding that mutually beneficial relationship,” explains Price. “They were able to ask what we need. Then we were able to flip it and say, "What role can we play to support your success.” “You come out the other end with everybody in a better place.” The revised Indigenous Content Playbook is now available. Download a copy here .

title: Everything Else Ends at Midnight. The Photos Don't.
summary: Booking a quality wedding photographer? Here's how to read portfolios, spot red flags, and lock in the one vendor you can't reshoot. Practical 2026 tips.
body_text: Everything Else Ends at Midnight. The Photos Don't. Anyone can nail golden hour. The real test comes in the dark reception hall. The flowers wilt. The cake gets eaten. The band packs up and the venue turns the lights on. A day you spent a year planning is over in about eight hours. What stays is the photographs, and that is the whole reason the person holding the camera matters more than almost any other choice you make. Couples already sense this. In Zola's 2025 First Look Report, 91% called social media an invaluable planning resource, and 68% said they vet vendors, photographers included, by scrolling Instagram and TikTok. The instinct is right. The method is where people get burned. A curated grid tells you someone can pick nine great frames. It does not tell you whether they can carry an entire wedding. Here is how to tell the difference. Why the word "quality" carries the weight With the average 2025 wedding now near $36,000 and 95% of couples saying it was worth every penny, the money is not really the question. The question is what you have left afterward. Zola found couples are most willing to splurge on an incredible photographer, ahead of the venue and the food, and the reason is simple: you cannot re-run the day. A caterer who underdelivers is a bad meal. A photographer who underdelivers is a gap in the only record you will keep. That is why "quality" is not a vibe. It is a set of things you can actually check before you sign. What a quality wedding photographer looks like on paper True-to-life skin tones are the tell of real editing, half of what you pay for. Start with full galleries, not highlight reels. Any portfolio looks strong at nine images. Ask to see two or three complete weddings, start to finish. Consistency across a whole day, from a dim morning hotel room to a dark reception hall, is the real skill. Anyone can nail golden hour. Look specifically for the hard moments. Backlit ceremonies, a first dance in near-darkness, candid reactions caught without a second try. If every image is a posed portrait in perfect light, you are seeing a narrow range. Check that faces look like faces. Skin tones should read natural and consistent shot to shot, not orange in one frame and blue in the next. Uneven color across a gallery is a sign of rushed editing, and editing is half of what you are paying for. Finally, make sure the style is genuinely theirs. Zola noted that the sense a vendor understands your vision is the single biggest reason couples pick one. If a photographer's work only sings in one aesthetic and it is not yours, that is a mismatch, not a flaw. Questions worth asking before you book A short conversation surfaces most problems. Ask these directly: • How many full weddings have you shot, and can I see one from a venue like mine? • Do you bring backup gear and a second shooter? • What is your turnaround time for the final gallery? • Who edits the photos, you or an outside service? • What happens if you get sick on the day? The answers matter less than the confidence behind them. A quality wedding photographer has a real plan for the day something goes sideways, because at some point something always does. The red flags No contract, or a vague one, is the biggest. So is no backup plan for gear or illness. Be wary of prices far below the local market, which usually means an inexperienced shooter or a subcontractor you will never meet. And if turnaround is quoted in months with no clear date, expect to wait. If the cost itself is the sticking point, our guide to what wedding photographers actually charge breaks down the ranges so you can tell a fair quote from a red flag. Booking without the guesswork The friction in all of this is time. Vetting portfolios, chasing quotes, and confirming availability across a dozen inboxes is its own part-time job during the months you have the least of it. That is the gap Snappr closes. Instead of gambling on a grid, you book a vetted professional in minutes, matched to your date and location, with the shoot guidelines and editing handled on the back end. The photographers are screened for exactly the consistency this guide describes, so the quality check is done before you ever reach out. Planning around a specific venue helps too; our roundup of beautiful wedding venues in Los Angeles is a good example of matching a photographer's strengths to a setting. Book a professional wedding photographer with Snappr and spend your energy on the day, not the vendor hunt. Frequently asked questions How do I find a quality wedding photographer? Look past the highlight grid. Ask to see two or three complete wedding galleries, check that skin tones and color stay consistent across the whole day, and confirm the photographer's style matches the look you actually want. A short call about backups, turnaround, and contracts tells you the rest. How much does a quality wedding photographer cost? Prices vary widely by market, experience, and hours of coverage. Rather than chasing the lowest number, compare quotes against your local range and treat a price far below it as a warning sign. Photography is consistently the vendor couples say is most worth the spend. When should I book my wedding photographer? Aim for nine to twelve months out, and sooner if your date lands in peak season or you have a specific photographer in mind. The best ones book first. If you are on a tighter timeline, on-demand platforms can match you with an available professional far faster. Sources 1. title: Governança Corporativa: como o controle de cartões individuais prepara sua empresa para auditorias e garante compliance financeiro
summary: Entenda como otimizar a governança corporativa de custos. Controle despesas por API e prepare sua empresa para auditorias rigorosas com o Stark Bank
body_text: Entenda como otimizar a governança corporativa de custos. Controle despesas por API e prepare sua empresa para auditorias rigorosas com o Stark Bank Toda empresa em crescimento enfrenta o mesmo desafio: quanto mais transações, mais difícil controlar. Gastos de viagem aprovados informalmente, compras feitas com cartões pessoais e notas fiscais acumuladas em gavetas comprometem a conformidade da empresa e têm impacto direto no processo de auditoria. Por isso, neste artigo, mostramos o que é a governança corporativa aplicada à tesouraria e como seus cinco pilares fundamentais se traduzem em processos concretos de gestão de despesas. Também exploramos por que o modelo tradicional de reembolso falha em auditorias e como cartões corporativos individuais geridos por API atuam como ferramentas ativas de compliance. Confira! O que é governança corporativa no cenário financeiro de scaleups e enterprise? No contexto da tesouraria, governança corporativa é o conjunto de políticas, processos e ferramentas que define quem pode gastar, quanto, em quê e com quais evidências. Trata-se de controle financeiro a fim de garantir que cada real movimentado seja rastreável, autorizado e conciliável. Para empresas em crescimento acelerado, muitas vezes essa estrutura acaba sendo negligenciada: o foco vai para a velocidade de expansão, e os controles internos ficam para depois. O problema é que o “depois” muitas vezes coincide com a chegada de um investidor exigente ou uma auditoria, momento em que a falta de rastreabilidade se transforma em passivo contábil. Por isso, crescer sem governança não é uma opção sustentável. Os 5 princípios da governança corporativa aplicados à gestão de despesas O Instituto Brasileiro de Governança Corporativa (IBGC) define cinco pilares fundamentais para a governança corporativa: Transparência, Equidade, Responsabilização (Accountability), Sustentabilidade e Integridade. Na prática da tesouraria, cada um deles tem impacto direto no dia a dia de quem gerencia gastos corporativos. Transparência: o time financeiro tem visibilidade em tempo real de onde o dinheiro está sendo gasto? Equidade: todos os colaboradores têm acesso a ferramentas adequadas para realizar compras corporativas sem precisar usar recursos próprios? Responsabilização (Accountability): é possível rastrear cada transação com documentação confiável e auditável, e prestar contas dela de forma clara e tempestiva? Sustentabilidade: a empresa tem visibilidade de como os gastos corporativos impactam sua viabilidade econômico-financeira no curto, médio e longo prazo? Integridade: a empresa tem políticas claras que evitam decisões de compra sob conflito de interesses, associando gastos a centros de custo e responsáveis? A maioria das empresas consegue responder “sim” para algum desses pilares. Poucas conseguem para todos, e é exatamente essa lacuna que compromete o compliance financeiro. Transparência e Equidade no controle de tesouraria de alta performance A falta de transparência no controle de despesas surge de processos fragmentados: aprovações via aplicativos de mensagem, compras feitas por um único cartão corporativo compartilhado, reembolsos que chegam semanas depois do gasto. O resultado é um painel financeiro que reflete o passado, não o presente. Mas o uso de cartão virtual corporativo PJ com limites individuais resolve a questão. Cada colaborador opera com o limite correto para sua função e o time financeiro enxerga cada transação no momento em que ela acontece, sem atraso, sem planilhas paralelas. A visibilidade síncrona do painel financeiro também atua diretamente na mitigação de fraudes, tornando anomalias detectáveis antes do fechamento mensal. Responsabilização, Sustentabilidade e Integridade sem atrito operacional A responsabilização (accountability) no contexto de despesas corporativas exige que cada transação tenha uma trilha documental confiável: nota fiscal válida, aprovação registrada e associação clara a um centro de custo e um responsável. Parece simples – e é, quando a infraestrutura é adequada. O problema do modelo clássico de reembolso é a fragilidade documental. Notas fiscais rasuradas, comprovantes de cartão pessoal sem identificação de categoria, aprovações informais que não deixam registro, tudo isso cria buracos na prestação de contas que, em uma auditoria formal, precisarão ser explicados. E explicações sem evidências custam caro: em tempo, em multas e em credibilidade. A integridade fecha esse ciclo: cada gasto precisa estar associado não apenas a uma pessoa, mas a uma política de despesas definida, livre de conflitos de interesse e coerente com os valores declarados pela empresa. Isso inclui regras sobre o que pode ser comprado, em quais categorias e com quais tetos. Quando essas regras existem apenas no papel e não estão parametrizadas nos sistemas financeiros, o controle depende de boa vontade, não de estrutura. Já a sustentabilidade entra na equação quando a empresa consegue enxergar como esses gastos impactam sua saúde financeira no curto, médio e longo prazo; não apenas no fechamento do mês, mas na trajetória do negócio. O calcanhar de Aquiles do compliance: por que o modelo tradicional de reembolso falha em auditorias das Big Four? O processo de reembolso por planilha tem uma grande fragilidade: ele é retroativo. O gasto acontece, o colaborador paga do próprio bolso, a nota fiscal é acumulada, o formulário é preenchido dias depois, o gestor aprova, o financeiro processa. Em cada etapa desse fluxo, há espaço para perda de documentação, divergência de categorias e inserção de dados com imprecisão. Em uma auditoria conduzida por companhias como Deloitte, PwC, EY ou KPMG, esse modelo gera inconsistências graves. Os auditores comparam os lançamentos contábeis com os extratos bancários e, quando os dados não batem ou a documentação está incompleta, o risco fiscal se materializa. Além disso, o uso de contas bancárias pessoais de colaboradores para despesas corporativas é um passivo tributário específico: a Receita Federal pode questionar a natureza dessas movimentações e exigir comprovação de que não se trata de renda adicional não declarada. A conciliação bancária automatizada é a solução direta para esse problema. Em vez de reconciliar dados depois, muitas vezes semanas após o fechamento do período, sistemas integrados permitem que cada transação seja conciliada no momento em que ocorre, eliminando o acúmulo no fechamento mensal e reduzindo o risco de relatórios inconsistentes. Como cartões corporativos individuais por API atuam como ferramentas ativas de governança A diferença entre um cartão corporativo convencional e uma solução gerida por API é a capacidade de parametrização em tempo real. Com o Cartão Corporativo do Stark Bank , o time financeiro não apenas emite cartões individuais, como também pode definir regras de uso para cada usuário ou categoria. Isso significa que é possível criar um cartão destinado exclusivamente a compras de mídia digital, com limite de R$ 50.000 mensais e bloqueio automático para qualquer MCC (Código de Categoria de Comerciante) fora desse escopo. Ou criar um cartão de viagens com teto diário definido, válido apenas durante o período de uma conferência. E essas parametrizações não dependem de aprovações manuais a cada compra, são configuradas uma vez e aplicadas automaticamente. O resultado prático está na tabela abaixo: Diferencial Operacional Sistemas de Reembolso Tradicionais Modelo Stark Bank Rastreabilidade de Gastos Retroativa, via notas acumuladas e planilhas manuais propensas a erros. Síncrona, com dados de transação gerados em tempo real direto no painel do banco. Mitigação de Fraudes Baixa, dependente de auditoria humana amostral pós-despesa. Alta, com regras de gastos pré-aprovadas, bloqueios instantâneos e validação via API. Conciliação Contábil Demorada, com fechamento contábil de até 15 dias após o período. Instantânea, alimentada por webhooks em tempo real integrados ao sistema contábil. Controle por Centro de Custos: organização contábil preventiva Um dos maiores gargalos no fechamento contábil de empresas em crescimento é a categorização retroativa de despesas. Quando os gastos não estão associados a um centro de custos no momento da transação, alguém precisa fazer isso depois e ainda manualmente. Já a segmentação preventiva resolve isso. Ao emitir cartões individuais já vinculados a centros de custo específicos, como Marketing, Recursos Humanos, Operações ou TI, cada gasto é automaticamente categorizado no instante em que ocorre. O orçamento de cada área é consumido em tempo real, e o time financeiro pode identificar desvios antes do fechamento do período, não durante. Para empresas com múltiplas filiais ou unidades de negócio, essa estrutura é ainda mais relevante: ela permite consolidar dados de diferentes operações sem depender de planilhas regionais enviadas por e-mail, reduzindo sensivelmente o tempo gasto na consolidação dos dados fiscais. Integração de despesas corporativas ao sistema de gestão: automação sem atrito contábi l O sistema de gestão empresarial é o núcleo contábil de qualquer empresa de médio e grande porte. O problema é que, no modelo tradicional, os dados de despesas chegam ao ERP com atraso: lançados manualmente, importados de planilhas ou digitados por um analista no fechamento do mês. Já a integração via webhooks muda esse fluxo por completo. A cada transação realizada com o controle de gastos corporativos com cartão , um evento é gerado em tempo real e enviado diretamente ao ERP da empresa. O lançamento acontece automaticamente, com as categorias e centros de custo já definidos. O impacto no processo de fechamento mensal é significativo: o acúmulo de consolidação cai, as divergências entre extrato bancário e sistema contábil desaparecem e a empresa entra no próximo período com os dados já conciliados. Para times financeiros essa mudança representa horas de trabalho recuperadas por ciclo. Impacto da Reforma Tributária: como manter a conformidade fiscal das despesas A Emenda Constitucional 132, promulgada em dezembro de 2023, instituiu a mais ampla reforma tributária do Brasil em décadas. A partir de 2026, o modelo atual de tributação sobre o consumo começa a ser substituído pelo novo Imposto sobre Valor Adicionado (IVA) dual: o Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS), de competência estadual e municipal, e a Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS), de competência federal. Para a gestão de despesas corporativas, a mudança traz uma exigência prática imediata: rastreabilidade documental de cada transação. A apuração de créditos tributários sob o novo modelo depende da vinculação entre nota fiscal eletrônica, transação bancária e registro contábil. Sem essa trilha completa e auditável, a empresa pode perder o direito a creditamentos que reduzem a carga tributária efetiva. Ou seja, a digitalização de documentos associada a cada transação passa a ser uma exigência legal. Assim, sistemas que capturam a nota fiscal no momento do gasto e a vinculam automaticamente à transação do cartão eliminam o risco de perda de documentação e garantem prontidão para a apuração de créditos sob as novas regras. Como implementar a governança de despesas com a infraestrutura do Stark Bank O Stark Bank é regulado pelo Banco Central do Brasil e é a primeira fintech do país a contar com avaliações das três principais agências globais de rating: S&P (brA-o), Moody’s e Fitch Ratings. Para CFOs que precisam justificar a escolha de um parceiro financeiro perante comitês de auditoria e conselheiros, esses critérios são diferenciais. A infraestrutura do Stark Bank permite implementar governança de despesas de ponta a ponta: emissão de múltiplos cartões corporativos com limites individuais, parametrização de regras por API, segmentação por centro de custos, integração com ERP via webhooks e captura de comprovantes em tempo real. Para scaleups que precisam escalar sem perder o controle e para enterprises que precisam manter o compliance em ambientes de auditoria rigorosa, essa combinação reduz a demanda operacional e garante prontidão para auditorias, sem depender de processos manuais ou planilhas paralelas. Se o seu time financeiro ainda enfrenta esses gargalos na gestão das despesas corporativas, esse é o momento de estruturar uma governança de verdade. Conheça o Stark Bank e descubra como implementar controles de gastos em tempo real na sua empresa. Perguntas frequentes sobre governança corporativa e compliance Qual é o papel da governança corporativa no compliance de despesas PJ? A governança define as regras de autorização de gastos de forma preventiva: quem pode gastar, quanto, em quê e com quais aprovações. O compliance garante que essas transações estejam em conformidade com os órgãos reguladores e com a política interna da empresa. Na prática, governança sem compliance é política sem evidência; compliance sem governança é auditoria sem estrutura de controle. Os dois precisam funcionar juntos. Como os cartões corporativos ajudam na preparação para auditorias das Big Four? O principal argumento em uma auditoria formal é a trilha digital. Cartões corporativos individuais com controles por API geram uma trilha de auditoria completa: data, valor, estabelecimento, categoria, responsável e centro de custo, tudo registrado no momento da transação. Isso elimina as divergências entre os dados bancários e os relatórios contábeis que auditores identificam como risco em modelos de reembolso manual.

title: How to Use AI Assistants to Build a Voice Call Automation | Circle
summary: Learn how to build a voice call automation with Circle Agent Wallet, AI assistants, and USDC to pay for services, place calls, and return proof of execution.
body_text: Agent workflows are easy to execute when they only generate text. They become harder when the agent needs to complete a real task end to end: find a service, pay for it, use it, and return proof of what happened. That is where many developer workflows break. The model may know the next step, but the application still depends on manual setup: creating accounts, adding payment methods, managing API keys, buying credits, checking balances, and stitching together receipts. Circle Agent Wallet helps developers build more autonomous applications by giving agents the ability to pay for services with USDC as a part of their workflow. Instead of relying on a subscription set up ahead of time, the agent can pay for access when it needs it. This unlocks composable workflows where agents can discover, purchase, and consume services on demand Consider a workflow where an AI agent monitors market conditions and needs to notify you immediately when sentiment changes. An email or dashboard notification may be too easy to miss, so the agent decides to place a phone call instead. To complete that task autonomously, it needs to acquire or reuse a phone number, pay for a voice API, initiate the call, and then return the call transcript, recording URL, and payment details. Rather than requiring a preconfigured account with the voice provider, the agent can pay for the service with USDC at the moment it needs it, allowing the entire workflow to execute autonomously from start to finish. Circle Agent Wallet works across AI coding tools and agent runtimes that can run Circle CLI commands or integrate Circle APIs. In this tutorial, we use Codex and Circle Agent Wallet to build that workflow end to end. You will build a workflow that: uses Circle Agent Wallet to pay for the services needed to place a call delivers a short market sentiment update to your phone returns the transcript, recording URL, and spend details for review runs the flow as a thread-bound heartbeat automation in Codex TL;DR setup If you want to try it first and read the breakdown after, start with this prompt in Codex: Use Circle Agent Wallet to set up a recurring voice-call workflow in this Codex thread. Config: - Your email: <EMAIL> - Destination phone: <PHONE_NUMBER> - Schedule: <SCHEDULE> - Auto top-up: 0.65 USDC per run, only if needed - Spending limits: calls up to $0.54 are approved; phone numbers up to $5.00 are approved only during setup; ask before anything higher or different. Goal: Call the destination with a short crypto market sentiment brief, then return transcript, recording URL, call status, and spend details. Setup: 1. Check Circle CLI is installed. 2. Check Circle Agent Wallet auth; if needed, start login and ask me for OTP. 3. List my Base Agent Wallet address. 4. Check Base USDC, service-chain USDC, and Circle Gateway balances. 5. Search for a paid voice-call service that supports my destination number; do not assume Base works for all countries. 6. Reuse an active wallet-owned phone number if available. If none exists, estimate cost and ask before buying. 7. Estimate call cost. 8. Place one short test call only after I confirm. Call style: Short, clear, neutral crypto market sentiment brief. Avoid hype. End cleanly. Max 1 minute. After the first successful call: Create a thread-bound heartbeat automation for the schedule above, continuing this same chat context. On each heartbeat: 1. Re-check auth, wallet address, balances, Gateway balance, caller ID, and call price. 2. Auto top-up only within the configured top-up limit if Gateway is low. 3. Place exactly one scheduled call if all checks pass. 4. Pause and ask if auth expired, terms are required, funds are insufficient, price changed, or phone number purchase/renewal is needed. 5. Return wallet status, services used, paid ledger, caller ID, call ID, status, transcript, recording URL, and total spend. Do not accept terms, buy/renew numbers outside setup, exceed spending limits, or place extra calls without required confirmation. The rest of this guide explains how the setup works and what to expect. Why Circle Agent Wallet is part of this workflow Without a wallet, a workflow like this usually breaks into separate manual steps: sign up for a telephony provider add a payment method buy a phone number provision the service trigger the call track what was spent Circle Agent Wallet changes that by giving the agent a way to hold USDC , apply spending limits, and pay for services in the flow of the task. Because USDC is programmable, the agent can acquire resources and complete work without a human manually provisioning every account or payment step. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: Access to the Codex app Automations available in Codex Node.js v20.18.2 or later Circle CLI installed A Circle Agent Wallet with up to 6 USDC available on Base or the chain required by the selected service A Circle Gateway balance, or a USDC wallet balance to top up Gateway when needed. Some paid services may use Circle Gateway for payment. Gateway is separate from your wallet balance: your wallet holds USDC onchain, while Gateway can make that USDC available for fast service payments across supported chains. Circle Agent Wallets require human authentication for key actions—including creating a wallet and adding or updating spending policies—to ensure agents operate within user-defined rules and controls. Authentication is email OTP-based, and sessions expire after 28 days, so the initial setup and periodic re-authentication will require your input. Step 1: Set up your Circle Agent Wallet Install Circle CLI: npm install -g @circle-fin/cli Authenticate your wallet: circle wallet login [email protected] Get your wallet address on Base: circle wallet list --type agent --chain BASE Fund the wallet with USDC: circle wallet fund --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain BASE --amount 10 --method crypto Check the balance: circle wallet balance --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain BASE Step 2: Understand how the payment step works Circle CLI supports x402 -compatible paid requests with: circle services pay <url> --address 0xYourWalletAddress --chain <SERVICE_CHAIN> The service chain depends on the provider. For example, A voice-call service may accept payments on Polygon even if your Agent Wallet is funded on Base. Circle Gateway’s unified balance handles the crosschain transfer automatically. For this voice workflow, those paid steps may include: checking or reusing a wallet-owned phone number buying a phone number if no active one exists topping up Circle Gateway for nanopayments placing the outbound call Step 3: Run the prompt in Codex Now ask Codex to set up the workflow. The prompt should tell Codex to: check that Circle CLI and Circle Agent Wallet are ready find a voice-call service that can call your phone number reuse an existing wallet-owned caller ID, or ask before buying one estimate costs before paying place one short test call only after you confirm return the call transcript, recording URL, status, and spend details create a thread-bound heartbeat automation after the first successful call A simplified starter prompt looks like this: Use Circle Agent Wallet to set up a recurring voice-call workflow in this Codex thread. Call <PHONE_NUMBER> with a short crypto market sentiment brief. First check that Circle CLI, wallet auth, wallet balances, and Circle Gateway are ready. Find a paid voice-call service that supports the destination number. Reuse an active wallet-owned caller ID if available, or ask before buying one. Before placing the first call, estimate the phone-number and call costs, then ask me to confirm. After a successful test call, create a thread-bound heartbeat automation for <SCHEDULE> so future runs continue from this same chat context. Each run should return wallet status, services used, paid-call ledger, caller ID, call ID, call status, transcript, recording URL, and total spend. Keep the call short, neutral, and hype-free. Do not accept terms, buy or renew numbers, fund the wallet, exceed expected costs, or place calls unless confirmation is required and given. Step 4: Turn the task into a thread-bound heartbeat After the first successful call, create a thread-bound heartbeat automation, not a separate cron automation. This keeps future runs in the same Codex chat context, so the workflow can reuse discovered states like the wallet address, caller ID, provider endpoint, payment chain, and spending policy. Step 5: Review the call outputs A strong run should return: wallet status services used paid-call ledger purchased phone number call ID transcript recording URL total spend What success looks like A good run should feel simple from your side: Codex checks whether the wallet is ready Codex finds and pays for the required services Codex places the call you receive the update Codex returns the transcript, recording URL, and spend summary Alternative patterns For recurring market briefings, you can run the workflow every morning or every week with different prompts. For escalation workflows, you can trigger the call only when something important happens. Wrapping up In this tutorial, you used an AI development tool and Circle Agent Wallet to build a recurring voice call automation that can pay for the resources it needs, place a call, and return the resulting artifacts for review. This is the larger shift behind agent commerce: agents are moving from planning work to completing work. Programmable USDC gives agents a way to acquire services, operate within user-defined spending limits, and return payment records as part of the task. title: Superblock Work Hubs for Jakarta Teams
summary: Jakarta’s workday is being redesigned around mixed-use districts Anyone who has crossed Jakarta between meetings knows the real cost of “just one more trip.” A short calendar gap can disappear into traffic, parking queues, lobby check-ins, and the mental reset needed before the next call. For professionals, founders, sales teams, and regional business travelers in […] The post Superblock Work Hubs for Jakarta Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: Jakarta’s workday is being redesigned around mixed-use districts Anyone who has crossed Jakarta between meetings knows the real cost of “just one more trip.” A short calendar gap can disappear into traffic, parking queues, lobby check-ins, and the mental reset needed before the next call. For professionals, founders, sales teams, and regional business travelers in Indonesia, the smarter question is no longer “Where is the office?” but “Where should work happen today?” That is where superblock hubs are becoming a practical workplace trend. Jakarta’s integrated districts combine offices, malls, apartments, hotels, transit access, gyms, clinics, and dining in one compact environment. Used well, these hubs can reduce wasted travel time, support hybrid teams, and give employees better places to focus between client visits, internal meetings, and deep work sessions. Why superblock hubs fit Jakarta’s workplace reality Jakarta has always been a city of movement, but not all movement creates business value. Teams often travel from home to headquarters, then to a client site, then back across town for an internal meeting. Each transfer adds friction, especially during peak commuting windows or rainy-season congestion. Superblock hubs help teams rethink the workday around proximity. Instead of treating the central office as the default destination, companies can create a network of approved work locations inside mixed-use districts close to employees, clients, and transit corridors. Jakarta’s commute challenge is a productivity issue Traffic is not just an urban inconvenience; it affects how many meetings can be held, how much focused work gets done, and how employees feel at the end of the day. The TomTom Traffic Index for Jakarta regularly places the city among the more congested major urban areas, making travel planning a real operational concern for businesses. For HR leaders and department heads, this turns location strategy into a performance lever. If a team can replace a 90-minute cross-city commute with a 15-minute walk from a client meeting to a workspace inside the same district, the gain is immediate. The same principle applies to business travelers arriving from Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Tokyo, or Bali. A visitor with meetings in Sudirman, Kuningan, or Senayan may not need a full-day office. They need a reliable desk, meeting room, call booth, and stable connectivity within reach of their schedule. Mixed-use districts match how modern teams actually work Jakarta’s business activity is increasingly clustered around integrated districts such as Sudirman Central Business District, Kuningan, Thamrin, Senayan, Kelapa Gading, Puri, and areas connected to MRT or LRT routes. These locations already support the daily routines of professionals who combine meetings, meals, errands, and focused work. Strong superblock hubs typically offer: Office towers, coworking spaces, and serviced workspaces within walking distance Food and beverage options suitable for informal meetings or quick team lunches Retail, banking, clinics, fitness centers, and daily services that reduce side trips Hotels or serviced residences for visiting executives and regional teams Better access to ride-hailing pick-up points, MRT stations, TransJakarta corridors, or parking facilities When a district supports both work and life needs, employees spend less time coordinating logistics and more time doing the work they were hired to do. How superblock hubs improve hybrid team performance Hybrid work in Indonesia is no longer only about working from home. For many teams, the more useful model is distributed access: employees choose the most suitable professional workspace based on their tasks, meetings, and location for the day. Superblock hubs make this model easier to manage because they provide a familiar, repeatable structure. A sales team can meet prospects near the client’s office, a product team can gather for a sprint review near a transit-connected mall, and a manager can book a quiet room for performance conversations without asking employees to travel to headquarters. Use hubs to cut dead time between meetings One of the biggest workplace inefficiencies in Jakarta is the “in-between” hour. It is too short to return to the office, too long to waste in a café, and often too noisy for serious work. Superblock hubs solve this by giving professionals a predictable place to reset. For example, a B2B account manager may start the morning with a client in Mega Kuningan, take a video call from a nearby workspace, meet a prospect over lunch, and finish proposals before heading home. The day stays productive because the work environment follows the route. This approach is closely related to the idea of placing workspaces near clients rather than forcing everyone back to a single hub. For more on this operational shift, see how near-client workspaces cut dead time . Create a better employee experience without overbuilding offices Employees value flexibility, but they also need professional settings. Working from home may be effective for individual tasks, yet it can be difficult for confidential calls, stable video meetings, mentoring sessions, or team collaboration. Cafés are convenient but inconsistent. Superblock hubs offer a middle path. Employees get access to work-ready spaces in locations they already use, while employers avoid the cost and rigidity of leasing large offices in every district. For Indonesia-based teams, this can be especially useful when employees live across Greater Jakarta, including South Tangerang, Bekasi, Depok, and West Jakarta. A distributed workspace plan can reduce unnecessary travel while still giving everyone access to professional infrastructure. Where Jakarta teams can use superblock hubs most effectively Not every workday needs the same type of workspace. The value of superblock hubs comes from matching the location and format to the business need. This helps companies avoid both extremes: forcing all work into one headquarters or allowing unmanaged workspace spending across random venues. For best results, teams should map the most common movement patterns in their organization. Look at where employees live, where clients are concentrated, where leadership meetings happen, and which districts are already part of the team’s weekly routine. Best use cases by team type Different teams benefit from hub-based work in different ways: Sales and account teams: Use work hubs near client clusters to prepare, debrief, and update CRM notes immediately after meetings. HR and people teams: Host interviews, onboarding sessions, and confidential conversations in neutral, accessible locations. Finance and legal teams: Book secure meeting rooms for document-heavy work when privacy matters more than a casual setting. Founders and entrepreneurs: Combine investor meetings, vendor calls, and focused execution days without committing to a permanent office. Regional business travelers: Work productively between hotel check-out, airport transfers, and meetings in different business districts. Freelancers and consultants: Upgrade from cafés to professional spaces when meeting clients or handling intensive project work. For companies with hybrid teams, the most successful patterns often start with one or two use cases. For example, a company may first approve hubs for client-facing teams, then expand access to project teams that need occasional collaboration space. District selection matters more than office size A common mistake is judging workspace strategy by square meters alone. In Jakarta, accessibility can be more important than size. A smaller workspace in the right superblock may outperform a larger office that requires long travel from clients or employees. When evaluating locations, consider: Distance to major clients, partners, and government offices Proximity to MRT Jakarta, TransJakarta, commuter rail, or reliable ride-hailing access Availability of quiet call areas and meeting rooms, not just open desks Food, prayer room, parking, and daily convenience facilities Safety, building quality, and ease of navigation for visitors Whether the district remains usable during peak hours and bad weather Jakarta’s transport development continues to influence where work happens. Companies can monitor official updates from the Jakarta Provincial Government and transport-related agencies to understand how infrastructure improvements may change commuting and workspace demand over time. Building a cost-smart strategy around superblock hubs Workspace flexibility becomes much more powerful when it is managed deliberately. Without a plan, employees may expense cafés, hotel lounges, day passes, and ad hoc meeting rooms in ways that are difficult to track. This creates hidden costs and inconsistent employee experiences. A good hub strategy gives teams freedom within clear boundaries. Employees know where they can work, managers know how budgets are used, and finance teams can see whether flexible workspace spending is replacing or simply adding to existing office costs. Turn scattered spending into visible workplace data Many companies underestimate how much they already spend on informal work locations. Small reimbursements may look harmless individually, but they add up across teams and months. They can also hide risk if employees handle confidential work in unsecured public settings. Common sources of hidden workplace spend include: Café bills used as unofficial workspace expenses Hotel lobby meetings for visiting teams One-off coworking day passes booked without approval Meeting rooms paid by individual departments Extra transport costs caused by unnecessary office returns If this sounds familiar, it may be worth reviewing how shadow workspace spend appears in hybrid teams . The goal is not to reduce flexibility, but to make it accountable. In a market like Jakarta, visible usage data can reveal which districts truly support productivity. If employees consistently book spaces in Kuningan, Sudirman, or Puri because those areas align with client visits, the company can adjust policy based on real behavior rather than assumptions. Compare hub access with traditional office expansion Leasing a full office can still make sense for headquarters functions, culture-building, and teams that need daily co-location. But for companies expanding across Jakarta or Indonesia, permanent leases in every strategic district may be inefficient. Superblock hubs work well when demand is real but variable. For example, a team may need eight desks in South Jakarta on Tuesdays, a meeting room in Central Jakarta twice a month, and occasional quiet space near the airport or a hotel district for visiting leaders. A flexible model handles these patterns without locking the company into unused capacity. This is similar to the financial logic behind fractional offices. While the market context differs, the cost-control principle is useful for Indonesian decision-makers too. Read how fractional offices support cost control to see how flexible access can complement permanent office commitments. Companies can also benchmark workplace decisions against broader economic indicators. The Statistics Indonesia site provides data that can help leaders understand employment, urbanization, and economic trends shaping workforce planning. How to implement a hub-based workplace policy Moving to a hub-based model does not require a dramatic office transformation. The best implementation usually starts with a focused pilot, clear rules, and regular review. This lets companies learn from actual usage before scaling across departments. The policy should be simple enough for employees to use and structured enough for managers to govern. If the process is too complicated, teams will return to informal habits. If it is too loose, the company loses visibility. Start with a 60-day pilot A practical pilot helps organizations validate demand before making larger decisions. Choose a few teams that travel frequently or struggle with long commutes. Sales, customer success, recruitment, and project teams are often good candidates. A 60-day pilot can include: Two to four approved districts based on client proximity and employee commute patterns Clear booking rules for desks, meeting rooms, and private call spaces Monthly budget limits by team or role Guidelines for confidential calls and document handling Feedback surveys on productivity, commute time, and workspace quality Usage reporting to compare actual demand with expectations At the end of the pilot, review both quantitative and qualitative signals. Look at booking frequency, popular locations, average session length, employee satisfaction, and whether transport claims changed. A successful pilot should show either time savings, better meeting outcomes, improved employee experience, or clearer cost visibility. Design rules that support trust and accountability Employees are more likely to use flexible workspace responsibly when expectations are clear. Avoid vague instructions such as “use when needed.” Instead, define the situations where hub access is encouraged. For example, companies may approve superblock hubs when employees: Have two or more client meetings in the same district Need a quiet place for video calls between external appointments Are attending a team workshop or offsite collaboration session Need a professional setting for interviews or performance conversations Are traveling from another Indonesian city and need a temporary work base It also helps to clarify when employees should not use paid workspace, such as for short personal errands, purely social meetings, or work that can be done effectively from home without disruption. Clear policy does not reduce autonomy. It protects it by making the model sustainable. What Jakarta can learn from regional workspace trends Jakarta is not alone in rethinking where professional work happens. Across Asia, dense cities are using malls, mixed-use developments, and transit-linked districts as flexible work nodes. The details vary by market, but the direction is clear: work is moving closer to daily life. This shift matters for Indonesia because Jakarta teams often balance global expectations with local realities. They need responsive workplace models that support international clients, regional travel, and domestic growth while recognizing congestion, neighborhood diversity, and employee wellbeing. Retail-integrated work is becoming a serious business tool Malls and mixed-use complexes are no longer just shopping destinations. In many Asian cities, they are becoming practical work environments because they offer safety, accessibility, food, parking, and extended operating hours. For employees, this reduces the friction of planning a full workday around multiple needs. The trend is especially visible in places where space is expensive and commuting is time-consuming. Hong Kong offers a useful comparison, where mall-connected work hubs help teams stay productive in dense urban districts. See how mall work hubs support Hong Kong teams for a regional perspective that Jakarta companies can adapt. For Jakarta, the opportunity is to use superblock hubs as part of a wider workplace ecosystem. Headquarters can remain important for culture and leadership, while flexible hubs handle distributed execution, client proximity, and intermittent collaboration. The future is not office versus remote; it is location intelligence The most effective workplace strategies will not simply ask employees to return to the office or stay home. They will use location intelligence to decide where different types of work happen best. That may mean: Deep work from home or a quiet nearby hub Client preparation from a workspace close to the meeting location Team rituals at headquarters on fixed days Leadership reviews in private rooms near central transit Regional visitor support through on-demand workspace access This model is especially relevant in Indonesia, where teams may be spread across Greater Jakarta and increasingly connected to clients across Southeast Asia. Superblock hubs give companies a practical way to support that complexity without overcommitting to fixed real estate. Make each workday easier to plan, easier to manage, and easier to justify For Jakarta teams, the best workplace strategy is not necessarily the biggest office or the most flexible policy. It is the one that reduces friction while keeping people productive, connected, and accountable. Superblock hubs offer a strong fit because they align with how the city already functions: business districts, malls, residences, hotels, and transport links working together in compact urban ecosystems. For employees, this means fewer wasted hours and more professional places to focus. For managers, it means better support for hybrid work without losing visibility. For finance and operations teams, it creates a clearer alternative to unmanaged workspace spend and underused office space. Start small, choose the right districts, measure real usage, and build a policy that reflects the way your people actually move through Jakarta. Done well, superblock hubs can turn the city’s complexity into a workplace advantage for teams across Indonesia. To book a workspace or download the free Deskimo app .
