title: Best Ways to Redeem Bilt Rewards Points
summary: Bilt points are worth about 0.55¢ as statement credit but 2–5¢ transferred to World of Hyatt, Alaska, and other partners. Every redemption ranked, all 16 transfer partners, and the sweet spots worth booking.
body_text: The quick answer What to actually do with your Bilt points Bilt points transfer 1:1 to a short but unusually good roster — World of Hyatt plus a set of airlines you can't reach from most other cards. That's the whole game. Redeem for statement credit or rent and a point is worth around half a cent. Move it to Hyatt or Alaska and it's worth 2¢, 4¢, sometimes more. The floor is low and the ceiling is high, so the exit is everything. The four rules that matter Transfer to travel partners. Never take statement credit, rent, or the Bilt Collection. World of Hyatt is the crown jewel: 1:1, with award nights from 3,500 points. On airlines, lead with the rare ones: Alaska, American, Flying Blue, Turkish, Aeroplan. Skip the Bilt Collection, Amazon, Lyft, rent, and Hilton/Marriott transfers — all well under 1¢. Roame fair value 2.05¢ per point A realistic average when you transfer to Hyatt or airline partners. Point value What your Bilt points are actually worth A point has no fixed value — it depends entirely on the exit. Bilt's built-in options set a brutal floor: the Bilt Collection merchandise store can price a paper-towel roll at 3,000 points, and statement credit hovers near 0.55¢. Transfers are the whole reason to hold the currency. Here's the spread you're choosing between every time you redeem. 0.3¢ Bilt Collection The true floor. In what world does a paper towel cost 3,000 points? 0.55¢ Statement credit & rent Rent runs ~0.7¢ (1.05¢ on Rent Day). Convenient, never worth it. 2–5¢ Hyatt & airline transfers Where the whole program pays off. Bilt has no travel portal that boosts point value — there is no 1.25¢ or 1.5¢ "book travel" tier the way Chase and Amex offer. The only route above 1¢ is transferring to a partner, which makes partner choice the single most important decision you make. Ranked Every redemption, best to worst The same points, ranked by what they're worth. Start at the top and only move down when availability forces you to. 1 World of Hyatt award nights Off-peak nights from 3,500 points; top-tier resorts that would cost $1,000+ cash. 2–5¢ 2 Alaska Mileage Plan partner awards Bilt is the only non-airline transfer partner. JAL, Cathay, and Qantas premium cabins. 2–4¢ 3 International business & first class Turkish, Flying Blue, Aeroplan, Virgin Atlantic. A $5,000 fare for ~60k points. 2–4¢ 4 American AAdvantage sweet spots A rare transfer route to AA — oneworld awards and web-special pricing. 1.8–3¢ 5 Accor Live Limitless (Rent Day) Fixed-value ~1.5¢ against Sofitel & Fairmont, best stacked with a transfer bonus. ~1.5¢ 6 Rent, statement credit, Amazon, Lyft, Collection You are leaving 65–85% of the value behind. The Bilt Collection is the worst at ~0.3¢. 0.3–0.7¢ Transfer partners Every Bilt transfer partner Points transfer to a compact roster — but a distinctive one. Everything moves at a clean 1:1 , and Bilt is one of the only transferable currencies that reaches Alaska and American . That rarity, not the length of the list, is the edge. Airlines · 11 programs Airline Program Ratio Why it matters Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan 1:1 The headline partner — the only non-airline currency that transfers into Mileage Plan American Airlines AAdvantage 1:1 Rare among transferable points; oneworld premium cabins Air France–KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Europe from 25k economy; monthly Promo Rewards United MileagePlus 1:1 Deep Star Alliance network and dynamic saver space Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 7,500 mi domestic United; cheap Star Alliance business Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Star Alliance, sub-500-mi economy from 6k points Virgin Atlantic Flying Club 1:1 ANA & Delta One sweet spots; frequent transfer bonuses Cathay Pacific Cathay 1:1 First & business to Asia with low surcharges Emirates Skywards 1:1 First-class shower spa to Dubai · watch surcharges Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 Star Alliance business with no fuel surcharges Southwest Rapid Rewards 1:1 Domestic economy at a fixed ~1.3–1.5¢; points count toward Companion Pass Hotels · 5 programs Hotel Program Ratio Why it matters Hyatt World of Hyatt 1:1 The crown jewel — award nights from 3,500 points IHG IHG One Rewards 1:1 Fourth-night-free and occasional cheap luxury nights Accor Live Limitless 1:1 Fixed-value ~1.5¢; ideal with a Rent Day bonus Marriott Bonvoy 1:1 Recently devalued — Bonvoy points worth far less. Avoid Hilton Honors 1:1 Honors points ~0.4¢ each — a steep downgrade. Avoid Hyatt is the only hotel transfer worth making by default. Hilton and Marriott convert 1:1 but their points are worth a fraction of a Bilt point — a straight downgrade. Accor is fixed-value (~1.5¢) and only makes sense against a specific stay, ideally stacked with a Rent Day transfer bonus. Sweet spots Four bookings that prove the point Real redemptions where your Bilt points go furthest — overwater villas, lie-flat seats, and Manhattan suites. Every one of these beats paying cash by thousands of dollars. Maldives ~5.4¢/pt World of Hyatt Park Hyatt · overwater villa 35k pts ~$1,900 value Off-peak nights at the Park Hyatt Maldives run 35k points against cash rates north of $1,900. The single most lucrative thing you can do with Bilt. Tokyo ~4.3¢/pt Alaska Mileage Plan JAL business · one way 60k pts ~$5,200 value Alaska prices JAL business to Japan at a flat 60k one-way. Bilt is one of the only ways to feed Mileage Plan without flying Alaska. Paris ~5.3¢/pt Flying Blue Business · one way 55k pts ~$2,900 value Standardized saver pricing to Europe from anywhere, and monthly Promo Rewards can knock 25% off award tickets before you even transfer. New York ~3.0¢/pt World of Hyatt Park Hyatt · category 7 35k pts ~$1,050 value A Manhattan Park Hyatt night for 35k points instead of $1,000+. Points earned paying your rent, going straight back into a stay near home. Avoid these The worst ways to use Bilt points Bilt makes these effortless because they're the least valuable to you. Each hands back most of your points' worth for the sake of convenience. If you're doing any of them, stop. Bilt Collection ~0.3¢ The merchandise store is the single worst option — everyday goods priced at multiples of retail. A paper towel for 3,000 points is not a deal. Statement credit 0.55¢ Wiping card charges hands back nearly half your points' value. There is no upside and no bonus tier. Never. Rent redemption 0.7¢ Using points toward rent lands around 0.7¢ (1.05¢ on Rent Day). Convenient, but a fraction of transfer value. Amazon "pay with points" 0.7¢ The most efficient non-travel exit — which is damning. Pay with the card and keep the points for a transfer instead. Lyft, fitness, student loans ~0.7¢ All the lifestyle redemptions cluster near cash-back value. Fine only if you genuinely will not travel. Hilton & Marriott transfers <1¢ They move 1:1, but the destination points are worth far less than a Bilt point. A voluntary downgrade — skip both. Earn more How to earn Bilt points fast The redemptions above are only as good as the pile of points behind them. The Bilt Card 2.0 lineup is now three cards — Blue, Obsidian, and Palladium — issued by Column N.A. and serviced by Cardless. All three earn on rent and mortgage with no transaction fee ; what differs is your everyday multipliers and perks. up to 1.25× on rent & mortgage — every card, no transaction fee Housing earning is no longer a flat rate. You pick one of two Bilt-exclusive bonus options that decides how you're rewarded: Housing-only rewards Up to 1.25× points on housing automatically, scaling with your everyday spend that cycle: 0.5× at 25% of rent, 0.75× at 50%, 1× at 75%, 1.25× when everyday spend meets or beats your rent. Below 25%, you still earn 250 points. Flexible Bilt Cash 4% back in Bilt Cash on everyday spend, on top of points. Redeem it dollar-for-dollar across Bilt, or spend $30 of Bilt Cash to unlock 1,000 points on a housing payment — up to 1× with no fee. Everyday Bilt Blue $0 no annual fee 1× Everyday purchases 2× Everyday spend on Rent Day (1st) Neighborhood Benefits: extra points at partner restaurants, fitness studios & pharmacies. Category maximizer Bilt Obsidian $95 annual fee 3× Dining or grocery — pick one yearly (grocery to $25k) 2× Travel 1× All other everyday purchases $100 annual Bilt hotel credit (semi-annual). Rent Day: 6× category, 4× travel. Premium Bilt Palladium $495 annual fee 2× Everyday purchases 4× Everyday spend on Rent Day (1st) $200 Bilt Cash + $400 hotel credit annually, plus Priority Pass lounge access. On Rent Day (the 1st of each month) everyday categories double, up to a 1,000-point bonus — 2× on Blue, up to 6× on Obsidian’s category, 4× on Palladium. All three carry a 10% intro APR for 12 billing cycles, no foreign transaction fees, and free credit reporting on rent. Earn rates and fees are published values; confirm current terms before applying. title: Video Call Hubs for Bangkok Hybrid Teams
summary: When Every Bangkok Workday Includes a Video Call A packed BTS platform, a sudden client escalation, and a calendar full of back-to-back video meetings can turn a productive Bangkok workday into a logistical puzzle. For hybrid teams, freelancers, and business travelers, the challenge is no longer whether people can work remotely; it is whether they […] The post Video Call Hubs for Bangkok Hybrid Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: When Every Bangkok Workday Includes a Video Call A packed BTS platform, a sudden client escalation, and a calendar full of back-to-back video meetings can turn a productive Bangkok workday into a logistical puzzle. For hybrid teams, freelancers, and business travelers, the challenge is no longer whether people can work remotely; it is whether they can join important calls with the privacy, audio quality, and reliability that professional work demands. This is where call hubs become especially useful. In a city where teams often move between homes, offices, coworking spaces, client sites, cafés, and transit corridors, having access to quiet, bookable spaces for video calls helps people stay responsive without sacrificing professionalism. For Thailand-based teams navigating flexible work, the right setup can reduce stress, protect confidential conversations, and make hybrid collaboration feel far more intentional. Why Call Hubs Matter for Bangkok Hybrid Teams Bangkok has become a practical base for regional teams, digital businesses, entrepreneurs, and global professionals working across time zones. The city offers strong connectivity, a deep service economy, and an increasingly flexible workplace culture. At the same time, hybrid work has exposed a very specific gap: people need more than a laptop and Wi-Fi to communicate well. Call hubs solve a common problem for distributed teams: where do you take a high-stakes video call when your home is noisy, your office is fully booked, or your next appointment is across town? Instead of relying on luck, teams can plan access to professional spaces that support focused communication. The Bangkok-specific friction points Hybrid work in Bangkok is shaped by the city itself. Traffic patterns, weather, dense commercial districts, and long commutes can affect when and where people work. A professional may start the day near Asok, meet a client in Sathorn, and need to join a regional Zoom call before heading to Ari or Ratchada. Without reliable call spaces, the default options are often poor: a noisy café, a hotel lobby, a car, or an open office corner where confidentiality is impossible. These settings can make even experienced professionals appear distracted or unprepared. Common pain points include: Unpredictable background noise from cafés, malls, and shared spaces. Limited private rooms in small offices or coworking areas. Video fatigue caused by poor acoustics and constant interruptions. Confidentiality risks during HR, finance, legal, or client conversations. Commute-related delays that leave little time to return to a main office. Hybrid work is now an operational design issue For HR leaders and business owners, the rise of flexible work is not only an employee preference issue. It is an infrastructure issue. Teams need clear systems for where focused work, collaboration, and confidential calls happen. Thailand continues to position itself as a destination for digital investment and regional business activity. The Thailand Board of Investment highlights the country’s role in attracting business and technology sectors, while the Digital Economy Promotion Agency supports the development of Thailand’s digital ecosystem. As more companies operate with distributed teams, the quality of everyday communication becomes a competitive advantage. In practice, this means hybrid teams need a network of places where people can step into a professional environment quickly. Call hubs are one way to make that possible without committing every employee to a fixed desk or expensive long-term office footprint. What Makes a Good Video Call Hub? Not every quiet-looking room is suitable for a professional video call. A proper video call environment should support privacy, comfort, stable connectivity, and a polished presence. This matters whether someone is pitching to an investor, interviewing a candidate, presenting to a regional leadership team, or discussing sensitive client information. The best spaces are designed around the reality that video calls are not passive tasks. They require concentration, reliable audio, confidence, and sometimes long periods of uninterrupted speaking. Core features to look for When evaluating call hubs in Bangkok or elsewhere in Thailand, focus on the practical details that directly affect meeting quality. A beautiful room is not enough if the audio echoes, the Wi-Fi drops, or people can hear every word from outside. Sound control: Look for enclosed rooms, acoustic treatment, or privacy pods that reduce background noise. Reliable internet: Stable Wi-Fi is essential, especially for screen sharing and multi-person video calls. Good lighting: Natural or well-positioned artificial light improves video presence and reduces fatigue. Comfortable seating: Longer calls require ergonomic support, not just a stool in a corner. Power access: Convenient outlets prevent the panic of a low battery before an important meeting. Easy booking: The space should be simple to reserve, extend, or cancel when schedules change. Professional surroundings: A calm, business-friendly environment helps people feel prepared and focused. For teams that use AI transcription tools or automated meeting assistants, room privacy becomes even more important. If meeting notes include client names, pricing discussions, or internal strategy, the physical environment should support data-conscious behavior. Deskimo has explored this further in why AI note-taking works best with private work rooms , which is especially relevant for teams handling sensitive conversations. Privacy is not a luxury feature Many professionals underestimate how often confidential information is discussed during routine calls. A sales update may reveal revenue targets. A recruitment call may include salary expectations. A client meeting may involve contracts, disputes, or future plans. In open environments, these conversations create unnecessary risk. Even if no one is intentionally listening, sensitive information can be overheard. For Bangkok businesses working with regional partners, regulated industries, or international clients, privacy standards can influence trust. “A professional video call space should protect both the person speaking and the information being shared.” This is why call hubs should be treated as part of a company’s hybrid work policy, not merely as a convenience. Just as businesses secure laptops and cloud systems, they should also think about where employees hold important conversations. How to Build a Practical Call Hub Strategy A strong hybrid work strategy does not require every company to build its own network of rooms. In fact, many teams benefit from a flexible model that combines home offices, company workspaces, coworking access, and on-demand private rooms. The goal is to match the workspace to the task. Not every day requires a desk in a corporate office, but certain meetings do require privacy and stability. A practical strategy helps employees know when to use which option. Map meeting types to workspace needs Start by reviewing the types of video calls your team takes in a typical week. Then decide which calls can happen from home, which require an office, and which are best suited to a professional room near the employee’s location. A simple framework can help: Low-sensitivity calls: Internal check-ins, informal updates, and non-confidential team syncs may be fine from home or a quiet open workspace. Client-facing calls: Sales meetings, onboarding sessions, and account reviews benefit from a polished, quiet setting. Confidential calls: HR matters, legal discussions, finance reviews, and executive meetings should happen in private rooms. High-focus calls: Workshops, interviews, training sessions, and board presentations require comfort, strong Wi-Fi, and minimal interruption. This approach prevents over-engineering. Employees do not need a private room for every conversation, but they should have access to one when the meeting requires it. Create location logic around Bangkok movement patterns Bangkok teams should design around mobility. A workspace plan that assumes everyone can return to one office between meetings may not reflect the reality of the city. Traffic, rain, school schedules, and cross-town appointments can quickly disrupt the day. Instead, think in terms of zones. Employees may need access to workspaces near major business districts, residential clusters, transit stops, and client locations. This is where distributed call hubs can reduce downtime. For example: A sales manager can take a regional partner call near Sukhumvit before visiting a client in Phrom Phong. A recruiter can book a private room near Silom for candidate interviews between office days. A founder can join an investor update near a transit hub instead of rushing back to a fixed office. A consultant can use a professional call room between meetings in Sathorn and Rama IX. Teams in other regional cities face similar challenges when meetings outgrow available office space. The operational thinking behind meeting overflow rooms for Singapore teams applies well to Bangkok too: flexible access can prevent scheduling bottlenecks without expanding permanent real estate. Best Use Cases for Call Hubs in Thailand Different professionals use private video call spaces in different ways. Some need them daily, while others only need them before critical meetings. The value comes from having reliable access at the moment work requires it. In Thailand’s hybrid work environment, call hubs are especially useful for roles that combine mobility, confidentiality, and frequent collaboration. For remote employees and hybrid teams Remote employees often enjoy flexibility, but home is not always the right place for every meeting. Family activity, renovation noise, pets, and shared living arrangements can affect call quality. For employees in condos or shared apartments, private work rooms offer a professional alternative without requiring a full-time office lease. Hybrid teams can use call hubs to support fairness. If some employees have quiet home offices while others do not, meeting performance may be influenced by personal living conditions rather than ability. Providing access to professional call spaces helps level the field. Useful scenarios include: Weekly one-on-ones with managers or direct reports. Regional team meetings across Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, or Australia time zones. Performance reviews and sensitive HR discussions. Online training, webinars, and certification sessions. Interviews and onboarding calls with new hires. For entrepreneurs, consultants, and business travelers Bangkok attracts entrepreneurs, consultants, and visiting executives who often work between appointments. For them, the question is not only where to work, but where to present themselves professionally on short notice. A café may be acceptable for answering emails, but it is rarely ideal for a board update or client negotiation. Hotels can be comfortable, but not always convenient or cost-effective for short calls. A bookable professional room gives business travelers more control over their schedule. Thailand’s economy is closely connected to tourism, services, manufacturing, and regional trade. The Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council provides economic data and national development context that underline Thailand’s role as a major business hub in Southeast Asia. As cross-border business activity grows, mobile professionals need work infrastructure that moves with them. There is also a lesson from transport-connected workspaces. When professionals can work near where they already are, they reduce the hidden cost of travel between meetings. Deskimo’s article on how transit hubs reduce workday friction explains why proximity can be just as important as amenities for modern workdays. How HR and Operations Teams Can Roll This Out For companies, giving employees access to call hubs should be simple, measurable, and aligned with business priorities. The aim is not to encourage unnecessary workspace spending. It is to make sure employees use the right environment for the right work. A clear policy helps employees make good decisions without asking for approval every time they need a quiet place. Set simple usage guidelines Start with practical rules that employees can understand quickly. Avoid making the process too bureaucratic, or people will return to poor workarounds like taking calls in hallways, cars, or noisy cafés. Guidelines might include: Use a private room for client calls where pricing, contracts, or strategy will be discussed. Book a quiet workspace for interviews, performance reviews, or sensitive HR conversations. Use professional call rooms for presentations longer than 30 minutes. Choose locations that reduce travel time between meetings rather than defaulting to the main office. Cancel unused bookings promptly so others can access the space. It can also help to define what employees should not use call rooms for. For example, deep individual work may be better suited to a regular desk unless privacy is required. This keeps availability high for people who genuinely need enclosed meeting space. Track outcomes, not just bookings The value of flexible workspace access should be measured by productivity and experience, not only room usage. HR and operations teams can review how call spaces influence employee stress, meeting quality, and travel efficiency. Consider tracking: Employee satisfaction with hybrid work arrangements. Frequency of missed or delayed calls due to commuting. Feedback from client-facing teams on meeting professionalism. Office room booking pressure during peak meeting hours. Reduction in unnecessary trips back to headquarters. Security-conscious companies can also learn from approaches used in other markets. For example, secure call pods for Australian hybrid teams highlights how privacy-focused spaces support distributed work without weakening professional standards. For Bangkok teams, the key is to make flexible access feel like a normal part of the work toolkit. Employees should know that when a meeting matters, they have a reliable option. Choosing Locations That Actually Improve the Workday The best workspace is not always the one with the most impressive design. It is the one that fits naturally into the employee’s day. In Bangkok, location strategy should account for transit, meeting routes, neighborhood density, and time-of-day movement. Call hubs are most valuable when they remove friction. If a person must travel 40 minutes to reach a room for a 30-minute call, the benefit disappears. A distributed approach works better. Prioritize proximity to work patterns Look at where your team actually spends time. This may include office neighborhoods, client districts, residential areas, and transit-connected zones. A workspace near BTS, MRT, or major road corridors can be more useful than a larger facility in an inconvenient location. For Bangkok-based professionals, practical location priorities often include: Access near central business districts such as Sathorn, Silom, Asok, and Phrom Phong. Options close to transit for employees moving between meetings. Availability near residential zones where remote employees live. Coverage near hotels and conference venues for visiting executives. Easy access to food, transport, and support services between calls. Small time savings compound quickly. If a team of 20 people each saves even one hour per week by using better-located workspaces, the monthly productivity gain is substantial. More importantly, employees feel less rushed and more prepared. Build a better meeting culture around space Workspace access alone will not fix poor meeting habits. Teams should also improve how they schedule and run video calls. A well-designed meeting culture reduces unnecessary calls and makes important ones more effective. Encourage teams to: Share agendas before meetings so participants can prepare. Use asynchronous updates when a live call is not necessary. Protect buffer time between meetings, especially for employees traveling across Bangkok. Choose private rooms for sensitive conversations rather than improvising. Respect end times so others can use booked spaces. The combination of better meeting discipline and better spaces creates a noticeable improvement. People arrive calmer, speak more clearly, and leave with fewer misunderstandings. Make Hybrid Work Feel More Professional and Less Complicated Bangkok’s hybrid teams need flexibility, but they also need reliability. The most effective work setup is not purely remote, purely office-based, or dependent on chance. It gives people access to the right environment at the right time. Call hubs help teams protect confidential conversations, improve video meeting quality, and reduce unnecessary travel across the city. They are useful for remote employees without ideal home offices, entrepreneurs moving between appointments, HR teams handling sensitive discussions, and business travelers who need professional space on demand. For companies in Thailand, the takeaway is straightforward: treat video call environments as part of your hybrid work infrastructure. title: How UVA Law Is Maintaining Visibility In A Direct Application World
summary: We recently sat down with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director of the Office of Private Practice at UVA Law, to discuss how UVA is navigating today’s evolving recruiting landscape.
body_text: A Conversation with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director, Office of Private Practice, UVA Law Like many law schools, UVA Law has watched law firm recruiting evolve rapidly over the past several years. As direct applications became increasingly common, the school made a strategic decision to move away from a traditional OCI structure and embrace a more flexible recruiting model. While the transition created new opportunities for students and employers, it also introduced a new challenge: re-creating visibility. Without bidding systems and centralized interview schedules, counselors emphasized individualized communication with students to continue to understand where students were applying, how engaged they were, and where they might need support. We recently sat down with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director of the Office of Private Practice at UVA Law, to discuss how UVA is navigating today’s evolving recruiting landscape and why greater visibility has become increasingly important as recruiting continues to shift toward direct applications . Q: UVA made the decision to move away from OCI. What drove that change? Emma : We were seeing more and more students apply directly to firms rather than through traditional recruiting programs, with many firms expressing their preference for this model. Flo shared data with us showing how much recruiting activity was already happening through direct applications, and it reinforced what we were seeing ourselves. Flo: As more schools experience similar shifts, many are evaluating how to support students in an increasingly direct application environment while reducing administrative complexity. For UVA, embracing that trend also created an opportunity to rethink how student recruiting activity could be monitored outside of a traditional OCI structure. Q: What was the biggest challenge after stepping away from OCI? Emma: We did lose some of the visibility that we would have otherwise had through hosting an OCI program. With OCI, you naturally have access to bidding information and interview schedules. You know who’s participating and where students are engaging. Once recruiting becomes more decentralized, you lose some of that built-in insight. We’re grateful that our students do such a wonderful job working closely with us every step of the process, but having a way to better understand where students are in the process at a glance would be incredibly beneficial for counselors and students alike. That’s where Flo Forward will help bridge the gap in visibility. Q: How has Flo Forward helped recreate that visibility? Emma: The application tracking and reporting tools are incredibly helpful. Being able to quickly see where students are applying, how many applications they have submitted, and whether interviews are progressing will help us have more efficient, productive counseling sessions focused on strategy and guidance. That visibility will help us identify where students may need support while also giving students time back that they may have been spending tracking their applications. Just having that snapshot is a win-win for all of us. Flo : As more students use Flo Forward to organize their job searches, that visibility continues to become even more valuable. Students can now track opportunities beyond those posted directly on Flo Forward, which will help schools better understand the full scope of their recruiting activity and have more informed advising conversations. We’re also excited to include Public Interest opportunities to the platform. Many students pursue a variety of career paths, and having more of those opportunities represented in one place will make it easier for students to stay organized while giving your office a more complete picture of how they’re navigating the recruiting process. This combination of student-driven tracking and advisor visibility helps create a more connected recruiting experience for both students and career services. Q: How has the Recruiting Tracker impacted your office? Emma: For several years, our team has spent countless hours creating our own internal resource that mirrors Flo’s recruiting tracker. Now, Flo’s recruiting tracker has taken the laboring oar of updating available opportunities, mitigating our need to maintain spreadsheets and search each firm’s website for current information. Q: How will you use the Event Board as part of your recruiting strategy? Emma : Recently, we updated our recruiting guidelines to allow firms more flexibility in hosting off-Grounds events with our students. We love working with law firms to help them plan out and schedule their events with our students, but are more limited in our ability to market each firm’s individual events, and don’t provide employers with class-wide student contact lists. The Event Dashboard helps firms promote opportunities directly to UVA Law students, while also providing us with visibility into student participation. Flo: Beyond employer-hosted events, schools can also add their own programming, creating a more centralized destination for students to discover recruiting opportunities. As students register through the Event Board, participation is shared back with the career services office, providing additional insight into student engagement and helping schools better understand which programming resonates most with their students. It’s beneficial for employers, students, and schools. Q: Recruiting timelines continue to move earlier. How does Flo Forward help students navigate that environment? Emma : Law schools operate on different timelines, and we constantly tell our students, “It’s a marathon, not a sprint.” If our students hear that their peers at other law schools are progressing in the recruiting cycle, being aware of those schools’ exam periods and grade release dates helps to contextualize their timing and encourage them to focus on running their own race. By bringing that information together in one place, the reporting ecosystem makes that context readily accessible. Q: What role does Flo Forward play in the overall student experience? Emma: One of the biggest benefits is centralization. Students are juggling applications, interviews, networking events, callbacks, and research across multiple employers and timelines. Flo Forward brings much of that activity into one place. Students can research employers, track applications, manage interviews, register for events, and stay organized throughout the process. Having a one-stop shop for students to send out their applications rather than navigating to every single law firm portal saves valuable time, and time is a limited resource in this accelerated cycle. Anything we can do to simplify the recruiting experience for students is a win. Q: As you look ahead, what are you most excited about? Emma : Overall, we’re just really excited to have a cohesive space for our 1Ls to conduct their job search, submit applications, and participate in interviews, that also gives us as CSOs real-time visibility into where they’re at in the process. Conclusion As law schools like UVA navigate the changing recruiting landscape, Flo Forward offers new ways to improve visibility into student recruiting activity while reducing administrative effort. Features like application tracking, the Recruiting Tracker, the Event Board, and enhanced reporting are designed to help career services teams spend less time managing processes and more time supporting students. title: Governance Is the New Moat: What the 2026 CSA Financial Services Survey Reveals About AI Adoption
summary: The 2026 CSA State of Cloud and AI for Financial Services report reveals a widening gap between AI adoption and the governance needed to control it, and why governance, not deployment speed, is becoming the sector's new competitive moat.
body_text: The question financial services institutions spent years debating — "should we move sensitive workloads to the cloud?" — has been settled. The conversation has moved on. What the 2026 Cloud Security Alliance State of Cloud and AI for Financial Services report makes clear is that the new question follows a similar trajectory, but is harder to answer: as AI agents begin to act autonomously inside financial systems, are your current controls enough? For most institutions right now, the honest answer is: not really. A Sector That Has Moved Faster Than Its Controls Sponsored by Anjuna Security, the survey drew 340 responses from security, cloud, compliance, and risk professionals across banking, fintech, insurance, and investment management, and captures a sector in the middle of an inflection point. First, cloud adoption is no longer lagging. It is infrastructure, even for regulated industries. Ninety-eight percent of financial institutions now operate cloud services. Sixty-four percent already store or process regulated financial data in public cloud environments, up from fifty percent in 2020. AI adoption has followed a similar arc. Just three years ago, the financial services sector was still tentatively running AI pilots. By 2026, forty-three percent of respondents report being in active implementation or advanced adoption. Only two percent report no AI usage at all. And yet the report surfaces a persistent and widening gap between how fast AI is being deployed and how mature the controls around it actually are. Twenty percent of respondents reported known AI-related security incidents. Another twenty-one percent are unsure whether incidents have occurred. That second number is arguably more alarming than the first. It suggests that a significant portion of the industry lacks the AI-specific monitoring and observability needed to know whether something has gone wrong — which is structurally different from knowing that nothing has. The Risk Is a Data Problem, Not a Model Problem When respondents were asked to name their top AI security concerns, the answer was unambiguous. Sixty-one percent cited sensitive data leakage through prompts, files, chat history, or other interaction vectors as their primary concern,m a figure that leads other concerns like adversarial model attacks, prompt injection, or data poisoning. This is an important framing shift. The dominant AI risk in financial services is not that someone will attack the model. It is that sensitive financial data will be exposed through ordinary usage: an employee pasting customer records into a public LLM for reconciliation, a RAG connector inadvertently surfacing data a user was never authorized to see, or a chat session retaining context that shouldn't persist. Cloud Security Is Not Just About Cloud The report finds that cloud security and AI security are no longer separable disciplines. The leading cloud risk such as third-party and supply chain concentration, and the leading AI risk — data leakage, at 61 percent — are not two unrelated problems. They are two expressions of the same underlying challenge: sensitive financial data now moves through more complex combinations of cloud services, external providers, AI models, retrieval systems, and autonomous agents than the original control architectures were designed to manage. Traditional security stacks including Security Information and Event Management (SIEM), Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) were built for virtual machines, containers, and APIs. They do not address prompt-layer leakage, vector-store exposure, model-in-use compromise, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) permission drift, or AI-generated output risk. But tooling is only part of the answer. The architectural question is whether sensitive data and AI workloads are protected at the infrastructure level, not just monitored at the perimeter. What the Data Recommends The report closes with a set of recommendations for financial institutions that converge on a clear set of priorities: Integrate AI risk management into cloud security governance, not as a separate side program, but as a unified discipline with shared telemetry and shared accountability. Treat data classification as a prerequisite control. Organizations that cannot reliably label sensitive data cannot govern what AI systems access, train on, or reveal. Deploy input and output guardrails; enforce access controls at the retrieval layer and monitor models and agents for drift, anomalous outputs, and extraction attempts. Extend exit and contingency planning to critical AI services, not just cloud infrastructure providers. Anjuna Security technology provides architectural value that software-only controls cannot match. As AI agents proliferate across financial operations, the need for a universal control plane that runs in Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) — one that can enforce runtime policy, maintain behavioral auditability, and verify the integrity of the environment where agents execute — becomes foundational rather than optional. This directly addresses the sensitive data leakage concern and the disparity between AI adoption and effective governance. The institutions most likely to benefit from AI will be the ones that build controls fast enough to match the pace of deployment, while maintaining the trust of customers, counterparties, and regulators. In financial services, trust has always been the business model. The next decade will depend on whether that trust can be extended to systems that increasingly act without a human in the loop, and whether the security architecture underneath those systems is equal to the responsibility. Download the full 2026 CSA State of Cloud and AI for Financial Services report to see the complete data set and benchmark your institution's controls.

title: Surfer SEO vs Ahrefs: Which SEO Tool Wins in July 2026

body_text: Most people comparing Surfer SEO and Ahrefs are asking the wrong question. It's not which tool is better. It's which problem you need to fix first. Surfer SEO is built to help content rank higher on Google and show up in AI search results. Its whole focus is on-page optimization: it scores your content against what's already winning in the SERPs and tells you how to close the gap. Surfer analyzes top-ranking pages for a target keyword, then hands you recommendations on keyword usage, structure, word count, and semantic term coverage. Write or rewrite, and the tool scores how closely your page matches what's already ranking. Beyond the Content Editor, Surfer covers keyword research, topical mapping, content auditing, rank tracking, and AI visibility monitoring. It's a content-first tool, not a backlink builder or technical crawler. What Is Ahrefs? Ahrefs is a data-heavy SEO suite built around backlink analysis, keyword research, rank tracking, and technical auditing. Where Surfer zeroes in on content scoring, Ahrefs covers the full search visibility stack: competitive research, site health, and historical link data included. Every plan includes Site Explorer, Keywords Explorer, Site Audit, Rank Tracker, and Content Explorer. The four tiers (Lite, Standard, Advanced, and Enterprise) differ mainly in usage limits and how deep you can go on crawl credits and tracked keywords. The pricing fits freelance SEOs, agencies, and mid-market in-house teams who actually use it daily. It's a research and monitoring product, not a content creation or execution system. That distinction matters once you start scoping what else you'll need to buy around it. Surfer SEO vs Ahrefs: Core Features Compared Surfer is a content optimization tool. It scores your pages against top-ranking competitors and tells you what to change mid-draft. Ahrefs is a competitive research engine: it shows you where your site stands and what's worth targeting before you write a word. The question isn't which has more features. Annual plans front-load all credits, which gives you more flexibility but locks you in. Add the AI Tracker and the real monthly number for a content team is closer to $194 than $99. Ahrefs Pricing Breakdown Ahrefs prices by seat count and data limits. Standard sits at $229/month, Advanced at $14,990/year (roughly $1,249/month). See how these stack up in a direct Maintouch vs Ahrefs comparison . The subscription price is the floor, not the ceiling. Ahrefs is a data product, it doesn't execute anything. You still need separate tools for content creation, outreach, and project management. Factor those in and the real monthly spend is materially higher than whatever plan you're looking at. Where Surfer SEO Falls Short Surfer scores your content and tells you what to change. It doesn't change it for you. Every recommendation requires manual execution, and that workload scales linearly, 30 articles a month means 30 manual optimization passes. The system doesn't learn from your edits either, so you're correcting the same patterns month after month. Beyond the content layer, the gaps compound. No programmatic backlink building . No technical SEO fixes. No CMS publishing. No internal linking automation. Understanding what makes high-quality backlinks matters more when you realize Surfer gives you no path to acquire them. A complete SEO operation means stitching three or four more tools around Surfer just to close the loop. Where Ahrefs Falls Short Ahrefs won't write your content, generate images, or push technical fixes live. It tells you what needs doing, then hands you a to-do list you have to staff and execute yourself. That gap between insight and shipped work is where most teams lose time, and money. For teams where programmatic backlink building is part of the strategy, that execution gap gets expensive fast. Who Should Use Surfer SEO? Surfer fits SMB teams that already have writers, editors, and someone managing the publishing calendar. If you've got editorial muscle in-house and need a scoring layer to tighten what they produce, it slots in cleanly. title: Give Your AI Agent Memory and Guardrails: Mem0 + Docker Sandboxes
summary: Add persistent memory to AI agents with Mem0 and Docker Sandboxes. Run local, private agent memory with Docker Model Runner, microVM isolation, and no cloud keys.
body_text: This blog is written in collaboration with Ajeet Singh Raina, Developer Advocate @Docker. Say you booked a flight ticket through an AI travel agent last week, and somewhere in that conversation, you mentioned that you're a vegetarian and you always go for an aisle seat. The agent took it all in stride and had you booked within a couple of minutes. When you come back this week to sort out the return flight ticket, though, it greets you as if the two of you have never spoken. You find yourself explaining the whole thing over again. That gap isn't a badly built app; it's how the model underneath works. Large language models (LLMs) are stateless. They carry nothing from one conversation into the next. They don't lay down memories the way a person does, so every session starts from a blank slate. Mem0 exists to close exactly that gap. Mem0 is an open-source memory layer that sits between your app and the LLM. Each memory is tied to an ID, a user, or an agent, so it recalls the right context for the right person. It works beneath any agent and any app those agents build, which is a compelling enough promise that 100,000+ developers are already building on it. Adding memory is the easy part. The part developers skip past is what happens next. That memory fills up with real details about your users and your work, and the agent reading and writing it usually runs right on your laptop, next to everything else you've got. We built this kit to fix that. It gives any agent a Mem0 memory layer, runs fully local with no cloud keys, and boxes the agent inside a microVM, so a bad day stays contained instead of spreading to the rest of your machine. How does Mem0 work? Mem0's flow splits into two paths, and the diagram follows both. Writing comes first. When a new user-and-assistant turn arrives, a single LLM call extracts the facts worth keeping and adds each one as its own record. This key design choice from Mem0’s latest algorithm only “adds”. It does not pause to decide whether each fact should overwrite or delete something older, which is what the previous version did. If a fact changes later, the new version is stored alongside the old one rather than replacing it, so the history of how something changed is never thrown away. From there, deduplication drops anything already stored, and entity linking tags the names, places, and things each fact mentions so related memories can connect later. Whatever comes through lands in the memory store. Reading is the shorter path, and it is where the token savings come from. A new question is scored against the store three ways at once: by meaning, by exact words, and by the entities it mentions. Those signals are fused into a single ranking, and only the handful of memories that actually matter are pulled back and placed into the prompt. Nothing replays the whole conversation, which keeps each call lean rather than growing with every turn. Here’s the quickstart: #Mem0 's hosted quickstart: store a couple of facts, then ask about them. from mem0 import MemoryClient client = MemoryClient ( ) # A short back - and - forth you want the agent to remember . messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I'm a vegetarian and allergic to nuts." } , { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "Got it, I'll remember that." } , ] # Save it under an ID for this person , so it comes back for them next time . client . add ( messages , user_id = "user123" ) # Later , ask in plain language and Mem0 returns the relevant facts . client . search ( "What are my dietary restrictions?" , user_id = "user123" ) #Mem0 's hosted quickstart: store a couple of facts, then ask about them. from mem0 import MemoryClient client = MemoryClient ( ) # A short back - and - forth you want the agent to remember . messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I'm a vegetarian and allergic to nuts." } , { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "Got it, I'll remember that." } , ] # Save it under an ID for this person , so it comes back for them next time . client . add ( messages , user_id = "user123" ) # Later , ask in plain language and Mem0 returns the relevant facts . client . search ( "What are my dietary restrictions?" , user_id = "user123" ) #Mem0 's hosted quickstart: store a couple of facts, then ask about them. from mem0 import MemoryClient client = MemoryClient ( ) # A short back - and - forth you want the agent to remember . messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I'm a vegetarian and allergic to nuts." } , { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "Got it, I'll remember that." } , ] # Save it under an ID for this person , so it comes back for them next time . client . add ( messages , user_id = "user123" ) # Later , ask in plain language and Mem0 returns the relevant facts . client . search ( "What are my dietary restrictions?" , user_id = "user123" ) Add that once, and the agent stops suggesting the peanut curry. Point the same thing at a coding agent, and it remembers your stack, your conventions, and the module that always breaks. And because it surfaces a handful of facts instead of replaying the whole conversation. In Mem0's research paper , the memory store holds about 7,000 tokens per conversation, where the raw history would run to roughly 26,000, which works out to more than 90% lower token cost and 91% lower p95 latency than passing the full context on every turn. What changes once memory is persistent? Useful memory fills up fast, and it fills up with things you'd rather keep an eye on. The vegetarian example is harmless. But the same store quietly collects preferences, past decisions, and, in regulated work, the stuff you really don't want loose, like patient history and allergies. So, before you wire memory into an agent, two questions are worth a minute. First, where does the memory actually live? With the hosted client from the quickstart, it goes to Mem0's cloud . For local development, or anything you'd rather keep on your own machine, the open-source version runs fully self-hosted. Second, and this is the one developer skip: what can the agent reach? The thing reading and writing to memory is usually running right on your laptop, as you, with your SSH keys, your cloud credentials, and a live network connection, all sitting within arm's reach. The kit answers both. For the first, it keeps everything local. For the second, that's where Docker Sandboxes comes in. Why run mem0 inside a sandbox? If you remember Mem0's enterprise checklist, it promised three things: your data stays yours, it runs locked down, and everything's logged. A Docker Sandbox hands a single developer all three, no enterprise contract required. Let's look at each one. Your data stays yours. By default, the kit runs both halves of Mem0, the model that extracts facts and the embedder that vectorizes them, on a local Docker Model Runner , and stores the vectors on local disk. Nothing about the memory leaves the machine. This local-first default isn't an outlier; it's where a lot of teams already are. Docker's State of Agentic AI report found that 61% of organizations run a mix of local and cloud models, and 39% run models locally in their own development environment. The reasons they give for keeping things local are the telling part: control and customization (61%), privacy and security (60%), and compliance (54%), with cost coming in a distant fourth. Memory is the most sensitive layer in the stack, since it's where user data and preferences accumulate, so it's the part you'd most want to keep on your machine. Running it on a local Docker Model Runner does exactly that. It runs locked down. A sandbox is a lightweight microVM with its own kernel and network namespace, and the only path it shares with your host is the project directory you mount. Everything trying to leave goes through a proxy that blocks by default, so the agent can reach only the handful of domains the kit declares and nothing else. You can see what that isolation means in about two seconds by opening a shell inside a sandbox and looking for the files you'd normally expect in a home directory: $ sbx run shell agent @ sandbox : ~ $ ls ~ /.ssh/ ; ls ~ /.aws/ ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.ssh/' : No such file or directory ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.aws/' : No such file or directory $ sbx run shell agent @ sandbox : ~ $ ls ~ /.ssh/ ; ls ~ /.aws/ ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.ssh/' : No such file or directory ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.aws/' : No such file or directory $ sbx run shell agent @ sandbox : ~ $ ls ~ /.ssh/ ; ls ~ /.aws/ ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.ssh/' : No such file or directory ls : cannot access '/home/agent/.aws/' : No such file or directory Those files aren't hidden or locked behind permissions. They just aren't in there. The agent has nothing sensitive to read and nowhere unapproved to send anything. Everything is logged. Every outbound request the proxy sees lands in sbx policy log , allowed or blocked, so you can look back at exactly what the agent tried to reach and when. Memory Poisoning Running memory locally and keeping the agent contained is good practice on its own. There's also a darker reason to do it. For years, the security worry with LLMs was prompt injection, and it was a contained one: the attack lived and died inside a single session. Persistent memory removes that limit, and the industry has named the result. OWASP added memory poisoning to its Top 10 for Agentic Applications as ASI06. The trick is that a bad instruction doesn't have to do anything right away. Something the agent reads, a tampered web page or a poisoned README, gets written into memory as if it were a normal fact. Weeks later, an unrelated question pulls it back as trusted history, and the agent acts on it then, long after the original message is gone and when nothing about the moment looks off. Researchers studying this have reported high success rates against production-style agents. To Mem0's credit, the project doesn't pretend this away. It offers per-user isolation, self-hosted deployments, and rules for what's allowed into memory, plus work on scanning content before it's stored. Those all guard the way in. What none of them cover is the moment a bad memory has already made it through, and the agent goes to act on it, and that's precisely where the sandbox earns its place. A poisoned memory can tell the agent to grab your SSH key and send it somewhere, but inside the VM, there's no key to grab and no open route to send it through. The containment turns a potential breach into a logged, blocked request. The Mem0 sandbox kit sbx-kits-mem0 packages all of this into one declarative file. It's a mixin kit, so it layers onto whatever agent you launch rather than defining a new one. wired to a local Docker Model Runner ( config at `~/.mem0/config.json` ) , so `Memory.from_config(...)` add / search works with no cloud keys or external vector database If you look at the following spec.yaml file, it might look overwhelming, but it's only doing five things: The network allowlist: A sandbox blocks outbound traffic by default, so the kit has to name the hosts the install actually needs: PyPI and files.pythonhosted.org for the pip packages, and the GitHub hosts for the spaCy model download. Nothing else gets through. (The one local exception, reaching Docker Model Runner on the host, you allow once in the Getting Started steps.) The environment: These are the variables Mem0's OpenAI client reads. OPENAI_BASE_URL points it at Docker Model Runner instead of OpenAI's servers, and NO_PROXY keeps those local calls from being routed through the sandbox proxy. The OPENAI_API_KEY: "dmr" looks like a secret but isn't, it's a placeholder the local runner ignores, there only because the client insists on some value. MEM0_TELEMETRY is off. The install step: Two commands. The first pulls in mem0ai with its NLP extras (the spaCy bits Mem0 uses to clean up extracted text), the second downloads the small English spaCy model. The --break-system-packages flag is just what pip needs to install into the sandbox's system Python. The config file: This is the heart of it. The kit writes ~/.mem0/config.json so that Memory.from_config(...) works the moment you're in the sandbox, no setup. It wires up three things: a local Qdrant vector store writing to disk inside the VM, ai/gemma3 as the model that extracts facts, and ai/mxbai-embed-large as the embedder, both pointed at Docker Model Runner. That's the self-hosted side of Mem0, not the hosted client from the quickstart. It's also marked onlyIfMissing , so if you tweak the config, the kit won't clobber your changes on the next run. The context note: The last block is a short note injected into the agent's context, so the agent itself knows the memory layer is there and how to call it. Put together, that's the whole promise: drop the mixin onto any agent, and it comes up with a working, fully local Mem0, models on your host, vectors on your disk, and no cloud keys anywhere. Getting Started Step 1. Installing sbx CLI The sbx CLI doesn't require Docker Desktop. Open your Mac terminal and run: $ brew install docker / tap / sbx $ sbx login $ brew install docker / tap / sbx $ sbx login $ brew install docker / tap / sbx $ sbx login Step 2. Turn on Docker Model Runner If you're on a Mac with Docker Desktop, turn on AI under Docker Desktop > Settings > AI, then pull the two models: docker model pull ai / gemma3 # LLM for memory extraction docker model pull ai / mxbai - embed - large # embedder ( 1024 - dim ) docker model pull ai / gemma3 # LLM for memory extraction docker model pull ai / mxbai - embed - large # embedder ( 1024 - dim ) docker model pull ai / gemma3 # LLM for memory extraction docker model pull ai / mxbai - embed - large # embedder ( 1024 - dim ) On Linux with Docker Engine, install Model Runner as a plugin first: $ sudo apt - get update $ sudo apt - get install docker - model - plugin $ sudo apt - get update $ sudo apt - get install docker - model - plugin $ sudo apt - get update $ sudo apt - get install docker - model - plugin Step 3. Launch the sandbox with the kit Layer the mixin onto an agent. The default tag needs no key: # DMR (default, no key needed) —: latest is the same as:dmr sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : latest shell sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : latest shell sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : latest shell Or straight from this repo over git: sbx run -- kit "git+https://github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git" shell sbx run -- kit "git+https://github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git" shell sbx run -- kit "git+https://github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git" shell Or from a local clone (the kit lives at the repo root): git clone https : //github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git sbx run -- kit ./ sbx - kits - mem0 / shell git clone https : //github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git sbx run -- kit ./ sbx - kits - mem0 / shell git clone https : //github.com/ajeetraina/sbx-kits-mem0.git sbx run -- kit ./ sbx - kits - mem0 / shell That's a shell session in a microVM with a working Mem0 memory layer, running entirely on models on your host. The shell on the end is the agent, and it's a separate choice from the memory backend, so you can swap in claude , codex , gemini , cursor , opencode , or anything else Docker Sandboxes supports without touching the memory setup. If you're using local default, then make sure you don't have a global cloud secret stored (sbx secret ls; remove with sbx secret rm -g openai). The proxy overrides the local dmr key with it, and Mem0's calls get redirected or blocked. Using a cloud provider Local is the default for a practical reason, and it matters most for Claude users. Mem0 has to have an embedder, and Anthropic doesn't ship an embeddings API , so a Claude agent has no cloud embedder in its existing credentials. Running it locally sidesteps that, and small local embedders like mxbai-embed-large are good enough now that retrieval quality holds up. Teams already paying for OpenAI or Gemini can use one key for both halves instead, and each provider ships as its own image tag with the right domains, install steps, and config already in place: Provider Runs where Credential Embed model Dimensions DMR (default) Local None ai/mxbai-embed-large 1024 OpenAI Cloud OPENAI_API_KEY text-embedding-3-small 1536 Gemini Cloud GOOGLE_API_KEY models/gemini-embedding-001 768 For the cloud tags you store the key once with the sandbox secret manager and the proxy injects it at runtime, so it never enters the sandbox: echo "$OPENAI_API_KEY" | sbx secret set - g openai sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : openai claude echo "$OPENAI_API_KEY" | sbx secret set - g openai sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : openai claude echo "$OPENAI_API_KEY" | sbx secret set - g openai sbx run -- kit docker . io / ajeetraina777 / sbx - mem0 - kits : openai claude One thing to watch when you switch providers: the embedding dimensions have to line up across the embedder config, the vector store setting, and the Qdrant collection, and Qdrant won't mix vector sizes in one collection. So changing providers means a fresh collection, either a new collection_name or clearing out the old store. Verifying it works One round-trip exercise the whole chain at once: the package, the config, the environment, and the link to the local runner. From the agent shell, save this to a file and run it with Python: cat > /tmp/ verify . py << 'EOF' from mem0 import Memory import json with open ( "/home/agent/.mem0/config.json" ) as f : m = Memory . from_config ( json . load ( f ) ) m . add ( [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I prefer dark roast coffee" } ] , user_id = "alice" ) print ( m . search ( "what coffee do they like?" , filters = { "user_id" : "alice" } ) ) EOF python3 / tmp / verify . py cat > /tmp/ verify . py << 'EOF' from mem0 import Memory import json with open ( "/home/agent/.mem0/config.json" ) as f : m = Memory . from_config ( json . load ( f ) ) m . add ( [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I prefer dark roast coffee" } ] , user_id = "alice" ) print ( m . search ( "what coffee do they like?" , filters = { "user_id" : "alice" } ) ) EOF python3 / tmp / verify . py cat > /tmp/ verify . py << 'EOF' from mem0 import Memory import json with open ( "/home/agent/.mem0/config.json" ) as f : m = Memory . from_config ( json . load ( f ) ) m . add ( [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I prefer dark roast coffee" } ] , user_id = "alice" ) print ( m . search ( "what coffee do they like?" , filters = { "user_id" : "alice" } ) ) EOF python3 / tmp / verify . py If the coffee preference comes back, memory is working end to end, with no cloud call anywhere in the loop. Real-world example: A Smart Travel Assistant Now that the Mem0 sbx kit is ready, let's pick up Mem0's own smart travel assistant demo: a personalized AI travel assistant that remembers the traveler across runs. The kit already did the setup the cookbook walks through. mem0ai is installed, the config is in place, and both the model and the embedder point at your local Docker Model Runner, so the demo comes down to running one script that ships with the kit as ~/runbooks/travel.py . Tell it something worth remembering: $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "I'm vegetarian, I like aisle seats. Book me to Lisbon." known so far : ( nothing yet ) ... the assistant books Lisbon $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "I'm vegetarian, I like aisle seats. Book me to Lisbon." known so far : ( nothing yet ) ... the assistant books Lisbon $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "I'm vegetarian, I like aisle seats. Book me to Lisbon." known so far : ( nothing yet ) ... the assistant books Lisbon The first run starts from a blank slate, answers, and quietly writes your preferences back to memory with memory.add . Come back in a brand new process: $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "Plan my return leg." known so far : [ 'Is vegetarian' , 'Prefers aisle seats' , 'Traveling to Lisbon' ] ... the assistant plans the return , without you repeating a thing $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "Plan my return leg." known so far : [ 'Is vegetarian' , 'Prefers aisle seats' , 'Traveling to Lisbon' ] ... the assistant plans the return , without you repeating a thing $ python3 ~ /runbooks/ travel . py "Plan my return leg." known so far : [ 'Is vegetarian' , 'Prefers aisle seats' , 'Traveling to Lisbon' ] ... the assistant plans the return , without you repeating a thing This is a separate process with nothing carried over, yet it opens already knowing the traveler, because the vectors live on the local disk inside the VM. Both the chat model and the Mem0 memory layer talk to the local Docker Model Runner , so it runs with no cloud keys . Usage ( inside the sandbox ) : python3 ~ /travel.py "I'm vegetarian, I like aisle seats. Strip it before any client is created . for var in ( "NO_PROXY" , "no_proxy" ) : if var in os .environ : os . environ [ var ] = "," . join ( e for e in os . environ [ var ] . split ( "," ) if e . strip ( ) != "[::1]" ) # sbx injects "proxy-managed" credential sentinels for openai / openrouter even # when no secret is configured . Mem0 's extractor reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the # environment , so the sentinel overrides the kit 's "dmr" key and the extraction # call gets routed to openrouter . ai ( which the sandbox then blocks ) . Force the # local key and drop the openrouter sentinel before mem0 is imported , so the # extractor stays pointed at the local Docker Model Runner . os . environ [ "OPENAI_API_KEY" ] = "dmr" os . environ . pop ( "OPENROUTER_API_KEY" , None ) from openai import OpenAI from mem0 import Memory USER = "traveler_123" # Chat model and memory both point at the local Docker Model Runner . llm = OpenAI ( base_url = "http://host.docker.internal:12434/engines/v1" , api_key = "dmr" ) with open ( "/home/agent/.mem0/config.json" ) as f : memory = Memory . from_config ( json . load ( f ) ) def reply ( question ) : # Load everything we already know about this traveler , not just query matches . profile = [ m [ "memory" ] for m in memory . get_all ( filters = { "user_id" : USER } ) [ "results" ] ] print ( "known so far:" , profile or "(nothing yet)" ) prompt = ( "You are a travel assistant.\n" f "What you already know about this traveler: {', '.join(profile)}\n\n" f "Traveler: {question}" ) answer = llm . chat . completions . create ( model = "ai/gemma3" , messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt } ] , ) . choices [ 0 ] . message . content memory . add ( question , user_id = USER ) # remember it for next time return answer if __name__ == "__main__" : question = " " . join ( sys . argv [ 1 : ] ) or "Plan me a trip somewhere warm." print ( reply ( question ) ) #! /usr/ bin / env python3 "" "A tiny travel assistant that remembers the traveler across runs. title: Ollama's highest performance on Apple Silicon yet with MLX
summary: Ollama's MLX engine has been updated to deliver its highest performance on Apple Silicon yet. Models output higher quality responses, respond faster, and use less memory.
body_text: Ollama’s MLX engine has been updated to deliver its highest performance on Apple Silicon yet. By leaning more heavily on Apple’s unified memory and the Metal-backed MLX framework, models output higher quality responses, respond faster, and use less memory. Your browser does not support the video tag. A coding agent with Gemma 4 12B on a MacBook Pro M5 Max. Ollama's improved MLX engine provides higher-quality results, higher output speeds and faster time to first token with thinking and multiple sub-agents. Higher quality responses with NVFP4 Ollama’s MLX engine has been updated to support NVIDIA’s model-optimized NVFP4 format, allowing for higher quality outputs than other 4-bit quantization formats while maintaining state-of-the-art performance. As an added benefit, models that are optimized for datacenter deployment can now be imported and run on with Ollama’s MLX engine allowing for portability between the datacenter and the desktop. NVFP4 tracks the local dynamic range of model weights more closely, reducing loss from quantization. When measuring the perplexity difference between q4_K_M , a common 4-bit quantization format available with Ollama, NVFP4, and unquantized bf16 weights for the Gemma 4 12B model, model-optimized NVFP4 roughly halves the quality loss while maintaining performance: Perplexity Gemma 4 12B – lower is better NVFP4 roughly halves the quality loss of 4-bit quantization, relative to unquantized BF16. Faster output performance Ollama’s MLX engine is now up to 20% faster from new optimizations: several operations are now fused into single Metal kernels via MLX’s just-in-time compiler features, and we’ve reworked Ollama’s GPU-backed sampling to run more efficiently. Output speed tokens/s · higher is better NVFP4 generates about 20% faster than q4_K_M on the updated engine. Average output speed over 10 runs when provided an 8,300-token input prompt. More responsive with agent workflows Agent workloads are dominated by prompt processing. Every tool call is a new request, and every request resends the whole transcript: system prompt, tool definitions, and every file read so far. Over a single task the model ends up processing the same context dozens of times. Prefix caching avoids the repeated work, as long as each request picks up where the last one left off. Real agent sessions don’t work that way for long. Ollama’s new snapshot system saves model state at key points across conversations, using the same approach that serves agent workloads in Ollama’s cloud: Multiple agents: An agent hands off to a subagent and picks back up later, or two sessions run at the same time. Each one resumes from its own saved state, and anything they have in common — often tens of thousands of tokens of system prompt, tool definitions, and ingested files — is only processed once. Thinking models: Reasoning tokens are generated, then dropped from the conversation history, so the next request never matches the state the engine just built. Each turn would normally reprocess the whole conversation. A snapshot taken right before the response starts gives the next turn somewhere to resume from. Branching and retries: A different follow-up or a regenerated response diverges from the cached conversation instead of extending it. Because snapshots exist where conversations split, only the new direction needs to be processed. Most new models make this harder than it sounds. Sliding-window attention and recurrent layers carry state that can’t be rewound. Once the model moves past a point in the conversation, that point can’t be recovered unless state was saved at the time. Ollama saves state at the points conversations are likely to return to: where they branch, at intervals through long prompts, and just before each response. Keeping snapshots selective and incremental leaves more memory for the model. Get started To run models with Ollama’s MLX engine, download the latest version of Ollama, then run a model: ollama run gemma4:12b-mlx For use in a coding agent, use ollama launch : ollama launch pi --model gemma4:12b-mlx

body_text: View All News GameSquare Repurchases Over 1 Million Shares in July 2026 07/23/2026 FRISCO, TX / ACCESS Newswire / July 23, 2026 / GameSquare Holdings, Inc. ("GameSquare" or the "Company") (NASDAQ:GAME), a next-generation media, entertainment, technology and digital native treasury company, today announced it repurchased over 1 million shares of its common stock during the month of July 2026 for less than $0.4 million, representing an average price of approximately $0.38 per share. Following this transaction, the Company has approximately $10.9 million remaining under its current authorization, which was expanded on April 14, 2026. Consistent with its capital allocation priorities, GameSquare intends to continue to opportunistically repurchase its common stock. Since October 2025, the Company has repurchased a total of over 8.8 million shares of its common stock for nearly $4.1 million, representing an average price of approximately $0.46 per share. "We continue to believe GameSquare's shares trade at a significant discount to the underlying value of our business, and we intend to aggressively capitalize on that disconnect through continued share repurchases," said Justin Kenna, CEO of GameSquare. "Our strong balance sheet, including capital generated through opportunistic ETH sales, provides us with the financial flexibility to pursue a highly active and aggressive repurchase strategy." About GameSquare Holdings, Inc. GameSquare (NASDAQ:GAME) is a cutting-edge media, entertainment, and technology company transforming how brands and publishers connect with Gen Z, Gen Alpha, and Millennial audiences. With a platform that spans award-winning creative services, advanced analytics, and FaZe Esports, one of the most iconic gaming organizations, we operate one of the largest gaming media networks in North America. As a digital-native business, GameSquare provides brands with unparalleled access to world-class creators and talent, delivering authentic connections across gaming, esports, and youth culture. Complementing our operating strategy, GameSquare has developed an innovative treasury management program designed to generate yield and enhance capital efficiency, reinforcing our commitment to building a dynamic, high-performing media company at the intersection of culture, technology, and next-generation financial innovation. To learn more, visit www.gamesquare.com . body_text: Official Statement: Wallbox Progressing New Capital Structure 2 min read As previously announced, on December 1, 2025, Wallbox initiated negotiations with its creditors as part of the implementation of a renewed capital structure agreed with its core banking partners and key shareholders.
